She orders the Sisters to come to Piacenza to be examined by the Vicar before their vows.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. I hear what you say about the Sister. Listen, please send me Sister A. Bartolomea, the one acting as Superior at Bagnacavallo, because they must make their vows; you can put her together with these, Sister A. Simeona, and [all] three for the feast of Saint Anne. Gather the Sisters wherever you think best, at Lugo or Bagnacavallo. I beg you, as soon as you receive this, send them at once: there are three.721

2. They need to be here early on Tuesday; they could arrive by the 4 a.m. train. So I hope you will do everything, because at 10 that same morning the Vicar is coming to examine them. Send them to me at once, for pity's sake.722

3. I wrote to you last night and it has already gone, so you will receive two almost together.723 Are you pleased? Goodbye till we meet, as you say, in 10 days. Come, for I cannot wait to talk with you. I am your

most affectionate mother Rosa

She has received the accounts, which are in order. She hears they are overworking to the detriment of their health and urges them to take care.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. I hear what you say.724 Earlier I received the accounts, and they are fine; as to the Sisters and the Superior, Salvatore had not mentioned it to me.

2. Listen, after the Saint's feast I will send them; are you pleased? Then you will see that they receive their salary.725

3. But I hear you are overworking, and that displeases me greatly, for I would like you to undertake only what you can; for pity's sake take care of yourself. Your health comes first, do you understand? The same for the Sisters, because those gentlemen, seeing you do everything, take advantage;726 for pity's sake, your health.

4. For the rest, I am so busy I have not a moment's breathing space, and I must leave you held close in my dear Crucified,

Your most affectionate mother Rosa

Worry about the grandchildren's health;

she invites them to come to her to avoid the epidemic.

A.M.F.

My dear son, dear daughter

1. I hear Nini is unwell; I am in a real state; moreover today Onorata came and told me there are cases in Genoa; for pity's sake come away.727

2. I am worried, for the coachman came to tell me the horse is ill; he sent for the vet, who says it is slight for now, but with all the talk, my God, I am really agitated, thinking of Nonnj and Nini... do not make me worry.728

3. Tell Sr. A. Benedetta I am not writing to her; I will see her on Monday. For pity's sake take care of yourselves, for I am worried. I will write again tomorrow. Goodbye; a kiss to Nonni and Nini; I am yours, affectionate M.R

The diploma examinations did not go well.

She warmly repeats her invitation for the feast of Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

Most Esteemed Professor

1. From your esteemed letter I gather your great disappointment that not all the diploma candidates were admitted to the oral examination. To tell the truth, knowing the ground as I do, you obtained even more than could be expected.729 This year they were poorly prepared, and despite your great efforts it was impossible to achieve everything.730

2. So you must not be discouraged; I assure you of my complete satisfaction, and you obtained even too much. Last year the candidates were more intelligent; this year they were somewhat lacking in understanding, or rather behind in their studies.

So I expect you for Saint Anne's day. That phrase of yours made me laugh — that your heart is not up to coming. That really is a good one! No, no. You leave it to me to remind you, and I absolutely want to. Not only do I remind you, but I repeat that I would be offended if you did not favour me on that day. I await you anxiously.

In the lively hope that you will grant my wish, I offer you my particular respects and remain with every esteem

Your

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

News, and an invitation to join her: prelates will be there to solemnise the feast of Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter

1. I received your letter. Now that you cannot bathe, would it not be better to come here? It has been cold for several days — I am not joking; I hear you are cold there too; so be cheerful, for pity's sake.

2. This morning at 4 the Bishop of Osimo arrived;731 so Bishop Scalabrini will say low Mass in the morning, the Bishop of Osimo will celebrate pontifical Mass at 10, and the Bishop of Borgo will sing Vespers — what do you think? And you not here? Why? Well, you know I would like always to be with you, don't you? Dear, dear ones, so patience.732 Write to me and believe me yours. Best wishes to Gaspare and a kiss to Nonni and Nini.

your most affectionate M.R.

Affection for her little granddaughter, whom she invites for the feast of Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

Dear Nonni

1. I do not know how to manage without my Nonnj. What are you doing — aren't you coming for Saint Anne's day? Come, you will see so many lovely things — what a beautiful feast!733 Dear Nonni, come and we will be together.

2. I am really sad that you have been left on your own.734 Detta and Giuseppina — Detta735 sends her love and says she misses you so much. Goodbye; come. Goodbye.

Your most affectionate Granny

Rosa

She repeats the invitation for the feast of Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

Dear Nonni

1. Just a line, as I really have too much to do. How are you? Dear Nonny, when are you coming? And soon. Oh, how long the days seem!736 I will tell you lots of things in person. Goodbye.

Your Granny Rosa

An exhortation not to complain or grumble, but to love Jesus and keep the holy Rules.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. From your letter I see you are complaining about the Superior, and that, I assure you, is very wrong; it is like complaining about God, for she is a real angel of a creature.

2. As for your suspicion that the letters you send me are being read, I assure you it is not true at all: I receive all yours, well sealed and in your own handwriting. I think you do very wrong to think this of your Superior; instead you should think about keeping the holy Rule, not waste time grumbling and watching what others do, but look to yourself, for you need it: having been long in religion, you should be the model of your community.

3. Meanwhile I will see about moving you to another house, and you, in the meantime, think about changing yourself, imploring the help of the [Saint] so that you never again displease her as you did by running off to the Bishop, and all those other scenes with the confessor.

4. My daughter, remember you must be grateful for the great benefits dear Jesus gives you; he loves you so much and wants to be loved in return. He calls you, and you do not answer?

5. Why so cold and ungrateful to such love? Love dear Jesus, my daughter; he alone can make you happy and content with the happiness the blessed enjoy in heaven.

So I want to receive a beautiful, most consoling letter from you, and to see in you the virtues a true Daughter of Saint Anne needs, as your most affectionate Mother

Rosa Gattorno wholeheartedly desires

She urges vigilance and observance of the holy Rules.

The two postulants are to be sent to Palermo with their dowries and certificates.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. Two lines in reply to your letter. I hear all is well and the Sister is improving. Keep a close eye on her.737

2. You could send the two postulants you have accepted to Palermo with their dowries and all their certificates, plus the travel money.738

3. I am very glad you had a fine feast for Saint Anne.739

Do well, and be very observant of the holy Rules.

4. Sister A. Francesca is well740 and sends greetings, together with Sister A. Benedetta and Sister A. Celsa.

Goodbye; the Lord make you a saint. I am ever your

most affectionate mother

Rosa G.

She thanks them for their good wishes and promises to pray for them: far away, yet present in her mother's heart and in the most sweet Heart of Jesus.

A.M.F.

My dearest daughters

1. Your good wishes for my name day are most welcome, as are your affectionate words, which I return with all my heart, saying with my whole soul: Be saints, all of you!!!

2. I never, never fail to pray especially for you; though you are far from me, you are always present to me in the most sweet Heart of Jesus.741

3. I hope none of you will forget to pray for me, for I need it.

4. The good news of your health, so dear to my heart, is a great consolation; let us thank the good God for all the graces he gives us, and you must use all this health for the greater glory of God and the prosperity of the Institute. I have nothing more to say now except to leave you with the Lord's blessing; believe me ever yours,

Most affectionate Mother

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

The Sister asks to change houses;

the Mother reassures her and urges her to do God's will.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. I see from your little letter why you want to change houses.742 Listen, you must be at peace about the Sisters and all they say about you; God's will is that you should stay in that house to become a saint. Always take your Superior's side, obeying her in everything, and pay no attention to anyone; be careful always to keep the holy Rule, and you will see what great consolations will rain down on you from heaven.743

2. So be at peace; I want to hear that you are content, for that is my consolation. Goodbye, my dear daughter; I leave you with the Lord's blessing; believe me for all ages

Most affectionate Mother

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She stresses the need for observance, backs the Superior's firmness and urges vigilance to keep good order in the various duties.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. From your letter I heard what you tell me about Sister A. Erminia.744 I absolutely do not allow her to learn reading and writing from Don Lentini. But tell me, my daughter, is that Sister going silly?

2. Does she not know that the Rule forbids any kind of familiarity with persons of the other sex? And how could I allow such intimacy? Listen, my daughter, you did very well to act as you did. Stand firm and do not permit so much familiarity with that priest. And if Sister A. Erminia does not behave well, as a true religious, let me know and I will find a way to bring her to her senses. Watch her as much as you can and tell me exactly how she behaves.

3. As for Sister A. Idelfonsa,745 certainly the Superior must keep an eye on everything and supervise the cook, the storekeeper, the nurses — everything — so that all goes perfectly and economically. Do you understand? Do not let the Sisters deceive you. Do your duty well, and above all keep up your vigilance.

4. Courage, my daughter; let us go forward keeping the holy Rules and being punctual at community exercises, and our holy Mother will pour out her abundant graces ever more.

I leave you with my blessing and am

Most affectionate mother Rosa

Instructions about the sick Sister: she is to take her to Palermo and ask Sr. A. del Salvatore for a replacement.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. Two lines in reply to yours. There was no need to get a doctor's certificate for the Sister;746 it was enough to tell me. So take her to Sister A. Salvatore in Palermo and ask for another.

2. As for the postulant, I will not accept her unless she has consent and her linen.747 Goodbye. I am in a hurry.

Be patient if I write little. The Lord bless you all.

Most affectionate mother

Rosa G.

The Mother apologises for not sending him the examination reports, which she has not yet received.

A.M.F.

Most Esteemed Professor

1. I have delayed writing until now in the hope of sending you the examination reports that the Superiors are sending in about their schools, but so far only a few have arrived and they cannot yet all be gathered.748

But I hope they will be ready on your return — if not all, at least a good number — and I intend to put them into your hands myself when you come back to Piacenza.

2. I am quite sure you are in perfect health, although I have reason to doubt it, since after you left I never heard whether you were alive or dead. Your work must keep you so busy that you have no time to breathe; or rather the pleasant holiday spot749 where you are must make you quite forget dull Piacenza, which is boring and melancholy enough. Be that as it may, once again I venture a request: that you come back soon to the house of the Daughters of Saint Anne, where I promise you excellent stews of potatoes and beans, and tasty, well-dressed salads of tomatoes,750 lettuce and so on. Are you pleased?

Meanwhile please accept the expression of my highest esteem; I remain

Your

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

Encouragement and an appeal for calm to avoid worse ills.

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter

1. I received your letter and see you are not at peace, although you tell me you are content. For pity's sake, my Carla, do not get upset. I wish you would not get so angry, because it can bring on bleeding. You know that; so do not get upset.751

2. I hope you will come soon, won't you? Come soon, I am waiting for you, for it is no longer hot here. Greetings to Gaspare and a kiss to Nonni and Nini, and believe me

Your most affectionate M. Rosa

She may keep the Sister as long as the work requires;

more Sisters will soon be sent to relieve them of so much toil.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. I hear what you say about the Sister; keep her until you no longer need her, all right? I am very sorry about your toil. Tomorrow the cook, the teacher and another assistant752 will leave here so that you need not wear yourself out.

2. For pity's sake, mind your health. If the ones from Naples come, keep them, and we will send them elsewhere later. Listen, everything you mention is ready, cloth and the rest.753 Goodbye; yours, in more than haste,

Affectionate M R.

Advice on the Sisters' health;

the postulants from Pontremoli are well.

A.M.F.

My daughter

I hear the Sister has arrived.754 See about having her accompanied, and whether she can stay with her sister for two or three days; if it did her good it would be worth staying 15 or 20 days. But if it did nothing for her, let her return to Genoa at once. You will see to it, won't you? The Pontremoli girls are all in good health and very happy.755 I commend the sick Sister to you; if you see she is not recovering, send her to Genoa.756 I have made myself clear, haven't I? Goodbye; your

Most affectionate Mother Rosa

The Mother urges her to trust in Saint Anne, who never fails to protect her beloved daughters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you say in your letter, and I am sorry to see that as soon as anything happens you all get into a state and lose heart, without any trust in God and our holy Mother, who has always shown her powerful protection to her beloved daughters when they turn to her with confidence.757

2. For the rest, be at peace: I will now try somehow to send your Superior back to you, and then, if her health does not allow her to stay, I will arrange to remove her.758

Goodbye; I leave you hoping you will do everything well and be content and at peace. Leaving you with the Lord's blessing, believe me ever your

Most affectionate Mother

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She should trust in Mary most holy, who will help her fight the adversary, and she will be victorious.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. I hear your conscience is troubled and you have no peace of heart. Listen, my daughter, you must not be cast down by this, for it is all the work of the infernal enemy, who wants to disturb your soul.759

2. When you are tempted like this, throw yourself into the arms of the most holy Virgin, who will protect you and help you fight the adversary and win a complete victory.760

3. So take heart and courage; I leave you with the Lord's blessing; believe me your

Most affectionate Mother

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

News of her brother's health, which is much better; there is nothing to fear.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. It really was a terrible moment. I had to leave at once for Rome, where, as you see, I am; thank you for your prayers.

2. My brother761 is better, and I hope he will continue so and have nothing to fear.

The point is that he handles all the business of the Rome house.762 Imagine! Goodbye; yours in my dear Crucified.

Most affectionate Mother Rosa

Rome, Vicolo del Piombo

She thanks them for the gifts and urges patience.

A. M. F.

Dear daughters,763

1. I am answering your two letters, which arrived almost together; I have not yet received the basket of grapes, but it will come. 2. I hear you cannot get any rice. Patience! I think you could go a little towards Switzerland, where it is not yet so cold; what do you say? I think you would do well.

I must stop, because the Americans are leaving. Ah, what work! My God! God bless you; believe me ever yours,

Most affectionate M. Rosa

Because of overwork she does not write often, but she is pleased with all her dear Irene does.

A.M.F.

My dearest daughter

1. If you saw me you would surely say: do not write, enough; but those who do not see me do not believe it; so that is why I am writing, only to tell you that I am pleased with all you have done and are doing.764 I wish you a thousand blessings. Goodbye; held close in my dear Crucified, I am your

Most affectionate Mother Rosa

She is worried about her health and urges her to look after herself.

A.M.F.

My daughter

In more than haste, two lines to ask how your health is.765 I received your letter through the Vicar and see you are still unwell. My God! how can it be? For pity's sake look after yourself and try to get really well. You speak of providence; if you need anything... In short, I urge you to get well at once. Goodbye; ever your

Most affectionate Mother Rosa

She is sorry about what happened to him in Florence and pleased with the excellent results.

A.M.F.

Most Esteemed Professor

1. From your letter I learned what happened to your leg near Santa Maria Novella. I was very sorry, but I hope you will soon recover fully.766

2. The consolation I felt in reading your letter was indescribable. At last we have reached our goal!

But it is all due to your zeal and energy... Otherwise who knows how much longer we would have had to wait.767

3. I look forward to a long, long letter from you, as you say in yours.

4. Meanwhile, so as not to bore you further, I close, thanking you infinitely and offering you all my service. I am honoured to remain your

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

News of the Sisters who left for America, full of courage and a truly admirable spirit.

A.M.F.

Most Worthy Count

1. Since the last Daughters of Saint Anne to leave for America768 are so dear to your heart, I enclose a letter received from Barcelona in which they describe their voyage and their immense sufferings.

2. You will read of the sufferings of those poor Sisters at certain moments, yet they are always full of courage and a truly admirable spirit. Read the enclosed letter and keep it as long as you like. Please accept the expression of my highest esteem and always consider me

Most Worthy Count, your

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

Note: From the Caracciolo Archive

Collegio Leoniano — Rome

Pos. Tornatore

She orders her to go to Putignano as pharmacist and encourages her not to be afraid but to trust in Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. Two lines to tell you that, as you will have heard, you are to leave on Wednesday for Putignano, where you will work as pharmacist in the hospital.769

2. So take courage and do not rely on your own strength; you will see that if you obey, our holy Mother will assist you with her grace and make you do everything well.770

3. So I urge you: do yourself credit and do not appear faint-hearted or ignorant; you will have to dispense the medicines and really act as a pharmacist.

I promise you I will always hold you close to my dear Crucified, that he may assist you. And do not be afraid.771

4. So I hope to receive great consolation from the Putignano house through my dear daughter, who will want to fulfil her Mother's wishes in every way.772

I leave you with my blessing and am ever your

most affectionate mother

Rosa G.

She thanks him for obtaining reduced railway fares for the Institute.

Most Esteemed Professor,

1. I was right when I said: "Anyone who wants to succeed in an undertaking should turn to Professor Alberti and he will obtain everything.

I was quite convinced that your efforts would obtain the reduction on the Southern and Roman railway fares, but not so soon.773

2. My gratitude is therefore infinite, and I assure you the whole Institute will remember it most gratefully. From your letter I learned that from 1 January applications for the reduction can be made freely, and even before — that is, from today — on application made and signed by me and Sister A. Santina to the respective directorates.

3. Without departing from what was arranged for the signatures, I would ask whether Benedetta Carrega could be put in place of Santina Solenghi, as that would suit me better, she being my secretary; and, without offending anyone, it would be hers by right.774 In your wisdom and prudence, see whether this could be done, provided it causes the Directorate no trouble. Otherwise I would rather leave everything as it is.

4. For the rest, the Te Deum will be sung on the day the Directorate General assigns us the form, and I want you to take part in the solemn service. What is more, there will be an exquisite ravioli feast,775 followed by choice wines of every kind. All the toasts and cheers will be for the Most Illustrious Cav. Prof. Francesco Alberti, who can rightly be called an eminent benefactor of the Institute.

In the lively hope that these last wishes of mine will be granted, I offer you my particular respects and, thanking you for everything, am honoured to remain your

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She does not agree about the Sisters to be sent to Pisa;

she will find suitable ones herself.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, look in the Pisa folder to see if there is a letter written by Count Desideri776 saying he leaves the house to the Sisters for 5 years; if you find it, register it and send it to the Superior Graziana.

2. As for sending the two Sisters to Pisa, the ones you mention are not at all suitable; I will think about it; I have none at present; I am tired; it is late. On Thursday evening I leave for Rome. Goodbye; your

Most affectionate M. R.

I have received your letters. Be of good heart; I hope you have given Count Camillo as much money as you could, since Gaspare is away; it is needed for the bill; please see to it.

She confides her displeasure at the news received.

A.M.F.

Most Reverend Professor

1. As soon as the form arrives from the Directorate General I will make sure to send it to you as you wish. I am, moreover, very upset to see from your letter that you are in a bad mood and not inclined to tell me the many things you say you ought to tell me. Enough. I hope that in your next letter you will tell me everything. Won't you?777

2. Please accept my respects and believe me

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She urges fidelity to the practices of piety and to poverty.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. I received the money order. All is well. So go ahead and make the shirts and please your Mamma.778

2. Be, always be cheerful and observant of the holy Rules; do not forget meditation; for pity's sake be punctual. Let poverty be your treasure. Goodbye; I hold you close in my dear Crucified and am yours for all ages.

Most affectionate Mother Rosa

Wishes for prosperity and happy days.

She cannot give news of the Americans' voyage.

A.M.F.

Most Illustrious Count

1. I have just received a letter from Federico and hasten to send it on to you.

What can I ever say to you for the very great favour granted to our poor Institute?

What fitting words shall I ever find to express my gratitude? I do not know; I feel utterly lost and unable to say what my heart would like to express.779 Encouraged by your kindness, however, I hope you will understand what I would like to say; and when the Father780 comes, everything in person.

I assure you I shall never forget you in my poor prayers, nor your most worthy brother. The whole community will offer fervent prayers for your prosperity and for very happy days.

2. I have heard nothing more of the Americans,781 either those who left or those about to come. Only the Superior at Sucre assured me in a letter that the Superior of La Paz had sailed for Italy with some other Sisters. But I do not know where they are now.

As soon as I have any news I will let you know at once. Father Tornatore is still at Paola, but is expected in a few days.

I close so as not to bore you further. Renewing my most heartfelt and fervent thanks, and offering you all my service with every esteem and veneration, I remain

Your

Most devoted servant Sr. A.

Rosa Gattorno

Collegio Leoniano - Rome

Pos. Tornatore

She is pleased with work well done; a new teacher will arrive.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. I am delighted to hear of the beautiful things you have done — well done! Courage; the fruit is certain; do not fear.782

2. So on Monday Sr. A. Admirabilis will leave for you, bringing all the diplomas with her. Do you always want to win?783 Hold fast to observance and you will see your enemies fall to the ground. Long live Saint Anne!

3. You answered the one from the nursery school well; let it sort itself out; do not worry. I am yours, holding you close in my dear Crucified; I am your

Affectionate M Rosa

She will send a good Sister whom the Bishop is expecting.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. Listen, for pity's sake, make sure Sr. A. Primitiva goes.784

2. For pity's sake — another good one will come to you; the point is that the Bishop is waiting for her. I beg you, do not let me down; do you understand?

Sure of your obedience, I am your

Most affectionate Mother Rosa

There is so much work that she cannot write in her own hand.

She urges her not to complain but to be cheerful and content.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Be cheerful, for I assure you it is not only to you that I do not write in my own hand, but to all in general; you can well imagine that the work keeps growing as the Institute keeps spreading; if you were at my side your heart would surely be moved to pity, seeing that I have not a minute to breathe.785

2. So please do not say such things to me again, for they hurt me deeply. I want to hear you are cheerful and content, always in the most sweet Heart of Jesus; leaving you with the holy blessing, believe me your

Most affectionate Mother

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She reports the Railways' reply, without objections, and asks after his health.

A.M.F.

Most Esteemed Professor

1. Here I am to report at once on the forms for the obedience requests.786

The Directorate General wrote to me fully approving the form sent and making no objection. So you can use the copies you took to Genoa, for your guidance.

2. I want to know how you are and whether you are still in such a bad mood.787 I have seen no more letters from you, which makes me fear some mishap. Write and tell me lots of things.

In the lively hope that you will oblige me, with every esteem I remain

Your

Most devoted Rosa Gattorno

Surprise at what has been written to her:

the devil's work, confusing things.

A.M.F.

My daughter

1. I am surprised at what you write. Evidently the devil has put his tail in it. I never meant to do that or to say it was untrue that you were suffering.788 Oh! what an ugly mug! (perhaps a Genoese term; she writes it often.)

God sees me, and he sees everything. I am overwhelmed with work and with... dear good! Sweet suffering! I am yours, poorest in soul and body, your

Most affectionate Mother Rosa

She will send the Sister to study.

Most Worthy Professor,

1. I have just received your kind letter and reply by return of post to tell you that I have also written to prepare all the Sisters to come here at once so as to have them ready, and if necessary I will telegraph; is that all right?

2. I hope you received my letter about the tickets.789

I can imagine how busy you are. Oh! what patience we make you exercise! The merit will be all the greater. I await your word, and they will be there at once.

3. Please accept a thousand thanks and more from your wretched

Most devoted Servant

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

She wants the church cleaned and the Sisters' quarters repaired.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter

1. I have just come out of church and a great thought has come to me; here it is. St. Francis is displeased that you are leaving his church and convent, and would like you to insist that they remove the damp and repair where you are living.790

2. Ah! what sorrow, to think that Jesus will no longer be so well cared for and honoured in that church — the Christmas night Mass, the Children of Mary, the lauds.

3. So think carefully about pleasing the Saint, and he will look after you.791 A prayer for your poor Mother, who remains ever your

Affectionate M R

She urges her to look after herself and not to overwork, assures her of her prayers, and promises to send the teacher soon.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter

1. I hear you have been so ill. For pity's sake, what are you saying! Why did you not have someone write to me? So do not overdo it; take care of yourself, rest, and do not worry.792

2. I always forgive everything; not only that, but in correcting you I always believe I am obtaining some good for your soul.

3. I will send you the teacher soon.793

If you knew what these days are like! Let it all be for Jesus. Pray that I may at last be converted, for I am always a real beast! Oh! pray!

4. When you are really well, if you think fit, come and fetch the Sister, but in that case after All Souls'.794 Goodbye; pray, and believe me yours in my dear Crucified,

Your most affectionate Mother Rosa

She sends on letters from America, knowing they will please him and make him smile.

A.M.F.

Most Illustrious Count

Most Worthy Count

1. Last night I received the enclosed letters and make it my duty to send them on at once; one will make you laugh, as she tries to write and makes blunders, with some Spanish words; the others are much the same.795

2. The Father has not yet arrived; I know he is in Naples.796 Trusting you are in good health — God keep you both for us.

3. Thank you for your letter. Warm greetings to Count Maurizio797 and Father Cirillo; believe me ever yours in my dear Crucified.

Most affectionate Sister

A. Rosa Gattorno

Note: From the Caracciolo Archive

Collegio Leoniano - Rome

Pos. Tornatore

She renews her thanks for all he does for the Daughters of Saint Anne.

A.M.F.

Most Reverend Professor

1. I am answering your very kind letter of yesterday, thanking you infinitely for all you always do for the daughters of Saint Anne, who will be grateful to you for ever.

1. Prof. FRANCESCO ALBERTI

Son of Benedetto and Maria Granara, born in Montoggio (GE) on 31.12.1828. A priest residing in Genoa, professor emeritus of the Andrea Doria Lyceum, librarian of the “Brignole De Ferrari” in Genoa. He knew Mother Rosa and was in contact with her from 1880 to 1900, for pastoral reasons linked to his office as a priest, in matters concerning the Institute in Genoa. From 1879 he gave his service free of charge in a community in Genoa. He was a witness at the Genoese process in 1918. He was a great collaborator of the Institute and in the professional training of the Sisters.

The correspondence between Mother Rosa and the Professor intensifies in the years 1882-1883.

He is considered by Mother Rosa a great benefactor of the Institute, and she invites him several times to spend the Feast of Saint Anne in Piacenza, at the Mother House, and to rest, regarding his presence as a gift.

He helps in the procedures so that the Institute may obtain the discount on the State Railways, and obtains it nationwide. Mother Rosa celebrates this great benefit with a solemn service and the singing of the Te Deum and, naturally, invites the Prof. to be present.

On one occasion Mother Rosa asks him to plead for the granting of the subsidy to the School of Sestri, and he obtains it. Many times Mother Rosa expresses gratitude and esteem for all he does for the benefit of the Institute: she thanks him for the Sisters’ qualifications, after immediate preparation given by him, and notes that he will always be remembered in the Institute for his dedication. Such is the trust Mother Rosa places in the professor that she writes to him: “I have no doubt of obtaining what you, Reverend Sir, are working so hard and with such pain to obtain”. If Mother Rosa, given her many continual occupations, has a letter written by a secretary, she assures him that she dictated it, so that its content is hers. When, out of weariness or discouragement, the “professor” decides to suspend his service and the Mother perceives his dejection, she encourages him not to think of death, explaining that the Institute cannot do without his precious support for the young Sisters. How would she obtain the Sisters’ “teaching certificates”, with so many schools open? He must not be disheartened if some sisters fail the examination. It happens that, despite his great commitments, the Sisters are poorly prepared. But she is satisfied with the results and with his labors.

2. DON GENNARO GRANITO DI BELMONTE

Gennaro Granito Pignatelli of the Princes of Belmonte was born in Naples on 10 April 1851, son of Angelo Granito, 4th Marquis of Castellabate, and of Paolina Pignatelli Aymerich, Princess of Belmonte, a great benefactress of the first communities of Naples. “Among the noble ladies who favored the Institute, one must remember Princess Granito Pignatelli of Belmonte who, having met Mother Gattorno, sought every way to help her Work. One day she introduced to her her young son Gennaro, who, among other gifts, had good artistic taste and knew how to wield the brush admirably. She therefore asked him to paint a picture of Saint Anne for the Sisters’ chapel. This picture, kept for many years in the Provincial house of Naples, is now in the Generalate in Rome. That occasion was the beginning of providential events in the history of the Institute, for if Prince Gennaro’s picture could recall the affection of his family, he himself, having become a priest a few years later, had with Mother Gattorno most precious spiritual relations. She herself gradually confided to him the work the Lord was prodigiously accomplishing in her and took him as counselor many times in her life.

Gennaro matured his religious vocation after attending, in September 1877, the funeral of the Archbishop of Naples, Cardinal Sisto Riario Sforza, who was reputed to be a saint. He was encouraged in his purpose by Don Guglielmo Sanfelice D’Acquavella, a monk of Cava de’ Tirreni, Riario Sforza’s successor in the archiepiscopal see of Naples. The latter would later ordain him a priest on 5 June 1879 and appoint him his personal secretary and administrator of the archiepiscopal curia (cf. Rosa Gattorno Fondatrice, pp. 295, 298).

It was in this period that Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte collaborated with the Mother to give life to the Sons of Saint Anne, a project that the Mother herself set aside, awaiting God’s time, because the corrections requested by Cardinal Sanfelice to the initial draft of the rule would have substantially altered what she felt she had received from God (Cf. Fisionomia Spirituale, pp. 294-297).

In 1893 he was called to the Secretariat of State. On 26 November 1899, Mother Rosa had the immense consolation of seeing her great friend and benefactor of the Daughters of Saint Anne consecrated Bishop, in the church of Maria Mater Gratiae, of the Generalate on Via Merulana. The ceremony was performed by the Secretary of State, Card. Rampolla, who agreed on that very occasion to become the new Protector of the Institute, Card. Verga having died shortly before. Mgr. Gennaro was soon afterwards appointed apostolic nuncio to Belgium.

In 1904 he was transferred to the Nunciature in Vienna and in 1911 created Cardinal. For many years he was also the beloved Protector of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

He died in Rome on 16 February 1948 and was buried in the Verano cemetery, Rome, in the chapel of the Capuchin Fathers, with whom he had a long, deep friendship as Cardinal protector.

IV. THE FOUNDATIONS (1882-1883)

1. ADERNÒ (ADRANO) (CT). Hospital – Poorhouse – Elementary schools 1882.

With the first house opened in Agrigento in 1876, the Daughters of Saint Anne had spread to many other towns on the island, giving their service mainly in hospitals, shelters and orphanages.

At the invitation of the Vicar Forane Salvatore Petronio Russo, and with the pastoral blessing of the Archbishop of Catania, Mgr. Giuseppe Dusmet, they arrived at Adernò (Adrano) on 28 January 1882. The three sisters, Sr. A. Basilia Marzocchi, Sr. A. Olimpia Epifania and Sr. A. Magna Pancheri, who had come from Palermo – where they had arrived by sea the previous day – were accompanied by Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi (Superior of the “Pignatelli” Institute), commissioned by the Mother Foundress.

The journey, rather long, was made in two stages. On the evening of the 27th they reached Catania and, since it was late, had to lodge with the very kind Sisters of Charity, to continue the next day, by carriage, to Adernò.

Before leaving they went to pay their respects to the Archbishop, who welcomed them kindly and asked for some clarifications about possible openings of houses in his City.

Sr. A. Crocifissa did not delay in giving the first news and wrote from Catania to the Mother about the conversation with the Archbishop and about some conditions for the future service.

“Today – she continues in the letter – we shall leave for Adernò. It is eight hours by carriage; the Archbishop says it is a most beautiful place, very populous. I say nothing more now; pray that we may make a good first impression and give edification of virtue. Please bless us all” (Letter of 28.1.1882).

With great precision, on the following 30 January, Sr. A. Crocifissa recounts in detail the particulars of the journey. On arrival they were received with much attention by the Vicar, who, with some of the most respectable gentlemen of the town, had prepared the beds for the nascent Community. However, the place to be assigned to the sick had not been settled, since there were two possibilities: the Capuchin convent and the Augustinian one. The Capuchin convent was inhabited by 24 old men, the Augustinian one by 9 sick people. The most suitable course was to unite the two groups and serve both at the same time.

Sr. A. Crocifissa has to stay several days for the conclusions, and will then return to Palermo. Meanwhile the sisters are lodged in the Capuchin convent together with the “poor old men”. She has confidence in the sisters, she feels them suited to the task to which they have been called; moreover, according to the Vicar’s intentions, schools and a boarding school are foreseen at the Benedictine convent, “very beautiful”. “If you saw – she continues in the letter – what fertility, it seems like the plain of Pistoia for the many things there are!” […]. We are in a town where there is everything: good meat, pasta, wine, excellent vegetables and all at little cost… Sr. A. Olimpia, who had a cough, these days no longer coughs; she is well”.

The leading group had met to take the final decisions: the hospital will be located in the Augustinian convent, because it is more spacious. Renovations and divisions of the wards are required, however, respectively for men, women, the old, the sick…

Sr. A. Crocifissa leaves again for Palermo, from where, on 7 February 1882, she completes the list of her information. “Yesterday I left the sisters of Adernò very well; before coming away I wanted to see them settled in the hospital, where there are 7 or 8 sick people, but kept like little animals, and there was a whole family to look after these poor invalids. Now, however, they have all left and the sisters will have everything under their direction … I left the masons to set up the wards to receive the sick and the poor old men, and within a few days they will unite the two communities, as soon as the wards are fixed. Everyone is fond of them. I hope everything will really progress well. I have already seen the fine building they will give for the schools, and they want them soon. Yesterday, as soon as I arrived in Catania, I went to greet the Archbishop and I cannot tell you the welcome he gave me again, saying to me: – We too want the Daughters of Saint Anne in Catania” (Letter of 7 February 1882).

Once Sr. A. Crocifissa had returned, the Vicar Russo himself – who had accompanied her to Catania by carriage, bearing the travel expenses – writes to Mother Rosa, grateful for the sisters’ coming, and accompanies his gratitude with the prayer “that this new plant, blessed by the Lord, in its homeland, may in the future bring to maturity fruits of sanctification to the greater glory of God”. At the same time he asks for the personal data of the certified sister, to include her on the Municipality’s staff roll as the appointments of teachers approach (Letter of 9 January 1882).

To the satisfaction of the good priest is opposed the dismay of the Superior, who finds herself amid a thousand difficulties: sharing the house with the family that attends the few sick, the lack of utensils necessary for the kitchen, the scarcity of linen; there are no napkins or garments to change the sick, there is no change even for the beds… and no immediate improvements are in sight. Sr. A. Basilia tries to press, but nothing moves and they are slow even to pay the salaries. The just complaints that reach the Mother make her aware of the situation. Poor Mother!

The sisters, only three, try to carry on, sustained by the help of God, of Saint Anne and by the spirit of obedience and, so as not to displease the Mother, agree to remain in Adernò, which, in the Superior’s words, “is the last town the Lord created and I did not know it existed” (Letter of 1 March 1882).

Mother Rosa encourages them, supports them, also changes the Superior and sends two other sisters: Sr. A. Demetria and Sr. A. Faustina, to cover the duties: school – sick – old people – kitchen.

The school is far from the hospital and it is a coming and going (four times a day).

Inspections by the school Authorities reveal the lack of qualifications; Sr. A. Demetria, who does not have the gymnastics certificate, is barely tolerated and very often has to endure mortifications and the threat of removal from the school. The poor sister complains to the Mother; she is not happy there and wishes to be assigned elsewhere. As for the pupils’ progress, it is not bad, but without the qualification she will not be able to teach.

In 1883 something has improved as regards the hospital, but as regards the school the difficulties persist over the regular appointment by the Municipality. Withdrawing all the sisters might be a solution.

The pressing appeal of the Vicar Russo obtains the postponement of the deplored decision and the change of other religious. The new presence of Sr. A. Gregoria Poppelman, a sister prepared and approved for teaching, solves the problem in part.

The school – as has been said – was distant, and this meant her absence from the hospital for many hours of the day; nor was it easy to reconcile the two things, also because whoever remained at home was not always able to fulfil the respective tasks for lack of instruction.

Some years later, in 1888, having left teaching, the community attended only to the hospital and the shelter. And in 1894, following open hostility from the anticlerical element, the sisters were forced to withdraw from the hospital too and then, always in agreement with the Rev. Provost Russo, they settled in a rented dwelling and opened there a private school of study and work, and a boarding school.

The Lord had made the field most fertile – watered with tears at the death of two sisters, Sr. A. Olimpia and Sr. A. Sionne – with numerous vocations; as we deduce from a letter of Provost Russo, dated 4 October 1889, the postulants who had entered among the Daughters of Saint Anne had reached the number of 20. Among them, the two sisters Anna and Maria Russo and Teresa Bua in 1886, and six other young women in a single expedition in 1889.

In the European conflict (1915-18), free as they were from all administrative dependence, with incomparable generosity they devoted themselves to helping and comforting families and combatants, adults and children, obtaining news, subsidies and other facilities, so that they became true consoling angels.

The Spanish flu found them on the front line, and countless were the visits of assistance brought to the homes of those stricken. For these merits of theirs, in 1920, the Prefectural Commissioner requested two more sisters for assistance at the Lazaretto for smallpox patients, and to them were subsequently entrusted again the hospital and the shelter, as well as the attached outpatient clinic.

Among the sisters who worked there, Sr. A. Gregoria Poppelmann is still remembered today, for her long residence in Adrano. Sent there by Mother Rosa in 1885 as Superior, she directed the Community and the works for the rest of her life. A sister of heroic virtues, favored also with extraordinary gifts, she flew to heaven on 2 March 1934.

Numerous testimonies from people who knew her have pointed out the privileges and charismatic gifts with which God had enriched “ZA NICA” (the little aunt, as she was called) and which accompanied her simple life, completely abandoned to the will of God. “A woman of prayer and penance” – as she has been described – she was unfailingly heard by the Lord, obtaining healings and graces for herself and for those who commended themselves to her in particular situations.

The Daughters of Saint Anne remained in Adrano caring for the sick for several more years, distinguishing themselves by their loving, tireless and boundless charity that characterizes their service.

The Agreement having expired, the Community, after some earlier attempts at closure, was withdrawn definitively on 29 December 1969.

2. PONTEDERA (PI). “Lotti” Hospital - 1882.

The negotiations for the settlement of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Pontedera (PI) take place through the provost Fr. Franco Conti, happy to have the sisters in his parish to assist the sick. Five sisters are requested, with the specific designation of Sr. A. Berarda Cattani, then Superior of the Community of Pisa (Letter of 28.02.1882). In a later letter the Parish Priest invites the Mother to go to Pontedera to visit the premises and settle everything in person, but to this proposal the Foundress replies that for health reasons she cannot and advises that he come to Florence to arrange everything (Letter of 3 March 1882).

Mother Rosa, while agreeing to send the first three sisters and later the other two, requires that some points of the contract be put in writing, promising at the same time that the sisters will be in Pontedera by 15 March 1882.

Their main duty in the “Lotti” hospital consists in assisting and serving the acute and chronic patients of the infirmaries. Excluded are only those services and treatments that are incompatible with the difference of sex.

The contract provides: “that the sisters be supplied daily with food, everything strictly weighed, and thirty cents a day each, the preparation of meals, attending to the laundry with the help of some woman who will be given them when needed. The cleaning of the entire Establishment is entrusted to the sisters. They may make use of the more able chronic patients as help in the services entrusted to them. In everything they shall depend on the “Master of the House” (Steward) and carry out his orders”.

Punctually on the appointed date the first three sisters arrive, and then the other two. They are:

Sr. A. Berarda Cattani

Sr. A. Astaria Amico

Sr. A. Perpetua Badocchi

Sr. A. Mistica Volti

Sr. A. Elvira Persiani

The Superior waits some time before giving news to the Mother. At first she observes what happens. There is much to do; the sick number 29 and the chronic patients 35 or 36. There is work for all without stopping a moment. The air is good and Sr. A. Berarda feels «risen almost to new life». The sisters are continually observed and checked; they have no say in the administrative side; the director physician sets their service shifts in the infirmary.

Something is not working. Sr. A. Mistica, of lively character, is not well regarded by the patients, who feel neglected. She herself, however, is able to justify herself to the Mother, because she is sometimes “hard of hearing” and, not hearing well, is not quick to serve them (Letter of 28.4.82). Some religious are changed, but the unease persists. We do not know exactly what happened, but it can be sensed that a struggle was waged against the sisters, from what we learn from a letter of Fr. Franco Conti who, with the greatest sorrow, comments on their departure from Pontedera.

«The devil has won, and these excellent Daughters of Saint Anne, after having done so much good to this Hospital, find themselves driven out by a disloyal, malicious, sectarian war. God has willed to give me a mortification too great and a harm to this people of mine. I adore His most holy will but I suffer. I did not suppose, Reverend Mother, that I had in the parish people so wicked as to commit such an action. I was too credulous about the establishment of this religious Family. And I let myself be deceived. Now I know it but too late, and I beg your pardon, Madam. Poor daughters, how many sacrifices, how many privations they had to suffer to benefit these patients and then find themselves repaid like this! God from heaven will reward their virtue. All did their duty, all, not one excepted» (Letter of 4 September 1882).

The presence of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Pontedera was very brief, not even a year. Despite the efforts at settling in and the commitment to a valid witness, at the end of 1882 they left the work.

Cf. AFSA Prot. 1881-86 D.4/37; M.4/32; Foundations).

3. PALERMO. Psychiatric Hospital - 1882.

The first request that reached Mother Rosa bears the date of 7 September 1877.

The president of the asylum, Dr. La Rosa, on the strength of information gathered about the praiseworthy charity practiced by the Daughters of Saint Anne in various towns of the island and in Palermo itself, turns to the Foundress to obtain four sisters, so that they may take on the task of supervision and care of the unfortunate patients of the psychiatric hospital.

In March 1882 he repeats the request, asking for five sisters: four will occupy supervisory posts and one will be in charge of the wardrobe. Lodging in the establishment, meals, clothing and an annual salary of £.360 are guaranteed.

Accompanied by Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi, with the task of Visitator, they reach the place on 25 March 1882. Nothing is ready; nevertheless the sisters adapt and set to work immediately.

Sr. A. Crocifissa represents the contracting party, sets the conditions and obtains that the five sisters not be separated in the two blocks “Porrazzi and Vignitella”.

A few days later she herself visits the sisters and finds them “all content with the service they perform.

Sr. Zenaide Sabini, in the midst of the patients on the way to recovery, keeps watch “like a soldier, without fear”, as does the Superior Sr. A. Elisa Corsini; the others always seem fearful and will adapt little by little. The work is not much for the sisters because there are attendants; it is a matter of keeping watch” […].

And in the letter of 11 April she writes: “As for the sisters at the hospital, they are very much loved by all; they would like three more for the other wing; they are a bit downcast because they must submit to the lay Governess and carry out what she orders them… There is not much work, it is a matter of keeping watch. I found the Superior in tears – she continues – she had received a reprimand from the Directress because they had let a mad woman out of her cell […] and a sister who was distributing the food had her veil torn to pieces… these are tasks that do not fall to them, but to the attendants… Sr. A. Fabiana received a blow to the head from a patient and they had to cut her hair to dress the wound” (Letter of 11.4.82).

The tone of the information given to the Mother by the Superior Elisa is no different. Her description does not mean to be a complaint; having no time for prayer, Mass only on Sundays, the night vigils, being unable to do the good one would like, all dishearten the spirits. The Administrators are not punctual in paying the salaries, the sisters need clothing, shoes, shawls, because having to go about the courtyards even at night they often get wet. Sr. A. Elisa asks for all this and mentions the purchase of an umbrella which they absolutely need.

Sr. Fabiana Orsi, sister of Sr. A. Del Salvatore, causes her great distress because, though not skilled in reading and writing, she has to keep up to date the registers of the entry and exit of the wardrobe garments and supervise the washhouse. Sr. A. Fabiana herself writes to the Mother to express her inability to fulfil the office entrusted to her, but says she is ready to obey, awaiting her coming to speak to her in person.

Sr. Guerina Gaudenzi thinks she cannot endure; she does not feel able to be among the patients. In one dormitory there are 82 patients, 80 in the other and the rest in small rooms; in all there are 280 patients.

In the following month of November other sisters are added and the community is divided between the two blocks: six at the central one and three at the branch.

In 1898 the general services were entrusted to the sisters, including the men’s wards, clothing stores, laundry, kitchen, pantry and sewing rooms.

In 1911, with the unification of the work, the management became easier and more regular, but how many heroic sacrifices the foundation had required!

The Agreement was renewed several times. The development of the work grew ever greater. The sisters increased in number over time (38-40); the staff assigned to care and custody about 600; the inmates 3000.

The sisters did great good there also from the spiritual point of view: baptisms of children born there to the demented women themselves, catechism, confirmations, first communions of young and adult inmates, marriages regularized of both patients and staff, conversions, abjurations of Turks and Protestants, practice of Christian life, frequent reception of the sacraments.

Naturally, as regards the patients, the work was limited to periods of calm and mental lucidity. The fruits were always copious; the spiritual peace that many enjoyed, after returning to God, had a beneficial influence on their psychic state and facilitated the recovery and normalization of their mental faculties.

Among the many sisters who succeeded one another it is obligatory to remember Sr. A. Aniceta Montanari, who, on 30 August 1884, was placed in the community as supervisor in the women’s sections and was then assigned to the direction of the laundry and wardrobe services.

“Vigilant and prompt, Sr. A. Aniceta drew attention by her goodness and energy of character. When in 1891 the post of Inspectress and Superior of the Daughters of Saint Anne became vacant, she was, by unanimous consent, assigned to that post, caring for the hospital’s economic interests and transforming the work into a noble apostolate of Christian charity. She was always the first to spend herself in the cholera epidemics (1885-87; 1893-94; 1910-1911) and in that of 1893, to comfort a dying nurse, she contracted the terrible disease through receiving in her mouth the patient’s spittle. For many days she was in danger of death, from which she miraculously escaped.

During the epidemic of 1918, which claimed so many victims in the Psychiatric Institute, she was a noble example to the staff and was the consoling angel of the poor sufferers.

Superior of this community for fully 58 years, as a mother and diligent educator, she died in Palermo on 30 October 1951.

Besides so many deserving sisters, one should also remember Sr. A. Guglielmina Gabbarelli, who in 1961 left earthly exile, leaving luminous examples of virtue: a marked spirit of sacrifice and self-denial, a boundless charity for the women patients entrusted to her care, to the point of no longer thinking of her own sufferings.

The Daughters of Saint Anne, after 108 years of service in the Psychiatric Hospital, left the work on 7 May 1990, accompanied by demonstrations of thanks and regret from the Administrators, the doctors, the staff and the patients.

AFSA Prot. 1881-86 D.5/40; M.5/34 Foundations

4. SASSUOLO (Mo). “St. Joseph” Orphanage - 1882.

The Work begins in 1882 (the first letter of the Superior Ma. Degli Angeli D’Alessandro is dated 16 May), at the request of Canon Agostino Ferri, who calls the Daughters of Saint Anne to direct the “St. Joseph” Institute, which houses some twenty abandoned orphan girls. The Archpriest G. Betti is pleased, feeling his heart expand at the thought of the great good that will be done in the town, and declares himself ready to give his help to the nascent Community.

Two sisters are requested, one of them certified, who will be assigned to the lower school classes, and the other capable of directing the kindergarten soon to open.

Mother Rosa agrees to send the sisters and Mgr. Ferri thanks her, describing at the same time the premises that will house the Community.

The institute comprises four rooms on the ground floor, one of which is used as a chapel; on the upper floor there is a large dormitory, in which twelve girls and three educators are currently housed.

They are very poor; they live on alms and on the collection, made by an educator and a girl weekly, which becomes more abundant at the time of the wheat and grape harvests. Later it will be the sisters who take care of this, as they will also be able to enjoy and administer the offerings.

Superior of the Community is Sr. A. Degli Angeli D’Alessandro, assisted by Sr. A. Vladimira, in charge of the collection, Sr. A. Evalda and Sr. A. Sion.

The sisters’ presence in Sassuolo did not last long. After 1887 there is no further news of the Work; it is therefore presumed that they were recalled by the Foundress.

AFSA, Foundations

5. ROME. Foundling nursery (Infants’ ward) - 1882.

In February 1881 a work had been established in favor of the women workers of the “Manifattura Sali e Tabacchi” (Salt and Tobacco Factory) in Piazza Mastai, 11 – Trastevere (see Mother Rosa Gattorno, Letters, vol. 6, pp. 685-686).

To this, in June 1882, a similar work was added, also in the Trastevere district, in via delle Fratte, 12.

The negotiations began through the interest of the Duke of Fiano, Marco Ottoboni, President of the Children’s Shelters. For this purpose the Commission commissioned the Marquis Francesco Serlupi to address a request to Mother Gattorno, asking her to grant her Daughters for the new work, within the month of June (Letter of 17.4.82).

Given the positive experience of the first house, Mother Rosa accepted the proposal and on 5 June 1882 the Agreement was stipulated, on the model of the one already existing: the sisters were entrusted with the direction of the shelter as well as the supervision, care and provision of every necessary attention to the said children, according to the regulations, and were paid an annual allowance of £. 425, oil, coal and £. 450 for the two maids of their choice.

The Foundress sent five religious there:

Sr. Bonifacia Pagniello as Superior, Sr. A. Agrippina, Sr. A. Domiziana Temporali

Sr. A. Urbana and Sr. A. Crisostoma

Sr. A. Berta Belliti, who directed the other work, assured the Mother that she would take an interest in the new house, teach the sisters who had arrived there, and help them in any need.

The news is satisfactory. “The sisters are doing well – she writes – and the Duke is pleased; he would like to entrust to the sisters the Kindergarten, for the moment run by lay people” (Letter of 11 June 1882).

Between the two communities a fine relationship of mutual help is established. “The other evening – Sr. Berta continues – we all went to look at the children and the sisters went to confession. We, by God’s grace, are all well and enjoy holy peace”.

Sr. A. Bonifacia Pagniello, for her part, reports on how the house is going: the children are 40-45, aged one to three, and all goes well although the house is not as “comfortable as Berta’s” (Letter of 12 August 1882).

And on 18 August she writes: “There is much to do, but we do it gladly; the sisters are content because we enjoy peace. If you saw, dear Mother, with what hunger (the children) come in the morning, they want to eat at once and have become so fond of us that they would like to be always with us; they come at half past six and leave at six in the evening. They give us everything we ask for and soon we shall have the garden. The sisters are all good, cheerful and work with pleasure; we enjoy such peace and do not feel the weight of the work”.

In April 1885, sisters and children move to other premises located in via Luciano Manara, 12, still in the Trastevere area. The house is not in good condition, so the Superior Bonifacia asks for modifications, which are generously granted. Extensions are made and safety measures strengthened, but from the hygienic point of view, in the judgment of the Superior Antonietta Gallinari, not all the due precautions were taken and, despite the cleaning done by the sisters, a certain bad smell is noticed right in the entrance hall, and it is necessary to point this out to Cav. Fabiani.

The sudden removal of the Superior is followed by Sr. A. Egista Patella who, “poor thing”, finds herself burdened with the reorganization of everything and with the resentments of the Duke, who complains of the lack of notice in the replacement of both the Superior and the sisters. Consequently the commission’s visits are more frequent and it is not rare for the sisters to be mistreated because the number of children is below 40, all pretexts being sought to seize upon.

The mediation of Gallinari was of no avail; she tried to calm both the Duke of Fiano and the Steward Fabiani, assuring them that the new arrivals would do well. The Cavaliere, recalling what had been done for three years to satisfy the Superior Bonifacia in all she had wanted, and “without regard to expense”, did not at all share the Foundress’s way of proceeding. It was the last straw. Through the cardinal vicar, Lucido Maria Parocchi, on 15 July 1885, the Duke gave notice of termination of the Agreement. This letter was followed by that of the Steward Fabiani, who confirmed the withdrawal of the sisters by the coming 19 October 1885 from the halls of the children’s shelter. Mother Rosa inevitably accepted the decision and assigned the five sisters elsewhere.

(Cf. AFSA Prot. 1881-86 D.4/37; 4/58 M.4/32; Foundations).

6. ROSSANO (CS). HOSPITAL 1882.

Once agreement was reached between Mother Gattorno and the hospital Board, after negotiations begun in March 1882 and the pastoral blessing requested from the Archbishop, the Daughters of Saint Anne arrive in Rossano in July 1882.

They receive an annual remuneration of £. 2500 a year, besides fuel, the furnished house and two cloaks a year.

The group is made up of six sisters, led by the superior Sr. A. Costanza Cenni. With her are: Sr. A. Policarpa Alessandri – Sr. A. Monica Prato – Sr. A. Ciricia Furogoni – Sr. A. Adalgisa Terroni – Sr. A. Rosalia.

On 7 July 1882, after the first days spent in a first arrangement of the various wards, the Superior communicates the first news to the Mother. They were welcomed with great celebration by the population. All are content, particularly the sick, who bless the Lord for their arrival.

The Superior certainly does not lack first worries: the hospital is full of dirt, and they have nothing left but to roll up their sleeves to give the wards the cleanliness that hygiene requires.

The hospital is large and the work great, to the point that they have no time to pray or sleep.

Sr. A. Policarpa is a real help. Sr. A. Costanza, animated by that firmness which is her own, manages to master the situation. The mother makes changes to improve the running of the hospital.

She consoles her daughter by instilling courage and recommending that she pray to Jesus, who always guides us (letter of 9.07.1882).

The labors increase also because the number of patients grows, distinguished by categories: soldiers, customs guards, carabinieri, railway workers… the poor. More sisters would be needed. Mother Rosa replies that for the moment she cannot satisfy the Superior; she tells her to wait; she will send as soon as possible two good, capable sisters, “since it is a matter of hospitals” (letter of 10.09.82).

Of the same tone is the letter of 10.10.82. The insistence of the Administration compels the Mother to provide – though not immediately – following new and better conditions in the financial treatment of the sisters.

Sr. A. Costanza, with an open heart, communicates her anguish and inner difficulties to her dearest Mother, who pours into her daughter’s heart the sweet balm of her reply: she will send her – if she is content – two novices (letter 19.10.82).

Alongside these anxieties, Sr. A. Costanza enjoys the assistance of the good God. With satisfaction she gathers the fruits of her apostolate: the confession of some patients at the point of death or of hostile soldiers who then yielded to the Lord’s Grace; the good running of the hospital; the goodness of the sisters, to the contentment of the Archbishop, the Administrators and the doctors.

The Daughters of Saint Anne, with the necessary rotations, continued their service of charity in Rossano until 1900.

AFSA Prot. 1881-1886 D.5/39.3

7. ORBETELLO (GR). “St. John of God” Hospital - 1882.

The first approaches for the opening of the hospital in Orbetello come through the mediation of Sr. A. Eugenia Gaudenzi, Superior of the Community of Montalto di Castro. Commissioned by Mr. Ciriaco Cecchini, a native and town councillor of that town, she writes to Mother Gattorno on 11 April 1882, reporting Cecchini’s intentions to take the hospital of Orbetello out of the hands of the «Freemasons» and entrust it to the religious. Sr. A. Eugenia faithfully conveys the petitioner’s thought: «He earnestly asks you to prepare for him six or eight religious for next June. Dear Mother, I hope you will do your best for this fine work. He says that a Superior is needed who knows how to keep her place and is courageous» and she presents its advantages, saying that the salary will be higher than at Montalto; the air is excellent and the house is larger and more comfortable, better suited to the needs of the hospital.

The negotiations proceed directly with Mr. Cecchini, who urges the Foundress to send her religious as well, as per the contract, once again recommending that the Superior be «well instructed».

The Agreement signed in August 1882 provides for an allowance of £. 3000 a year payable in monthly installments of £. 250 each, and, once only, travel expenses. The sisters may use the premises, duly furnished, as well as the kitchen, and have medical and surgical care, oil and firewood free of charge.

The sisters arrive in Orbetello on 15 August 1882.

The Superior assigned to the new community is Sr. A. Fulgenzia Bocciarelli, assisted by:

Sr. A. Eufrosina Laurella

Sr. A. Carolina Padroni

Sr. A. Perpetua Torielli

Sr. A. Verisfina Lodigiani

Sr. Zaveria Borella

Sr. A. Dell’Immacolata

to whom, after a few months, is added the excellent Sr. A. Amante La Barbera.

Important is what emerges from the surprising and at the same time lively description by Sr. Eufrosina, dated 18.8.1882, from which we learn some details of the beginnings of this “Pious place”.

She writes thus: «I am writing to give you news of this place, which I do not know how it is. Listen well. I came with the firm will to do good and to do myself credit with my poor work, but it is not possible for me to continue. Listen. We found a most horrible place, in the utmost filth, not only lacking everything, everything, even our rooms are (not) provided with anything but a plain straw mattress. So you can imagine what there is to do. Well, we had to set to work at once and not look at whether we were tired or not from the journey. The first day was spent in sending away at once the old attendants and turning everything upside down, that is, moving the patients (who are 18) from one big ward to another to clean, carrying beds up and down. We worked with all our might and all submitted willingly, but now it is different, the great workload is continual and even growing».

The tone of the letter, as can be seen, is very discouraging. The sisters’ complaints are frequent and weigh heavily on their behavior, which degenerates into slowness, inattention, quarrels with the patients and with the labourer, incompetence in service, even to the “sad figure of imbeciles”.

Sr. A. Eufrosina, with a touch of pride, though not daunted by the work that falls to her (the registers are rather difficult), does not tolerate poor showings, feels exceedingly downcast and it is not “possible that she will last”.

Beside this rather sad news, there is a minimum of consolation. I did not even believe – she continues in the letter – «that Sr. A. Verisfina would manage so well».

The necessary change of some sisters, wanted also by the Administrators themselves, changed the face of the community, but also of the hospital, which from a state of neglect rose to new life: order, cleanliness, discipline reigned everywhere and above all the poor patients were no longer deprived of those spiritual and material helps they needed.

Edified by this, moved by the charity with which the sick were cared for, the population of Orbetello blessed the Lord and, encouraged, began to resort to hospital care, previously so abhorred. It was not rare that through the sisters’ charitable work true conversions to God occurred, from whom some people had been estranged for very many years, and new vocations for the Institute.

The letter sent by the Superior Sr. A. Fulgenzia bears the date of 24 October 1882; a letter that decidedly has a different tone and lets us sense that the atmosphere has become truly breathable. She writes some months late, because she wants to give the Mother more reassuring and at the same time consoling news.

« Dear Mother, if you knew what consolation I feel in finding myself among these poor sick, I cannot properly express it; the sick are 38, we have work enough. My Mother, I go about all day and moreover I always keep watch; it is already three nights running that I have spent the night awake; I would never have believed that the Lord had given me so much spirit and health in this hospital. […] The sick become good every day, they obey me at the slightest sign. In truth I tell you I have nothing to complain of in anyone. The President comes every day, what I ask of him he denies me nothing; in a word, all are attentive and are fond of me […]. We all get along together and I have only to thank the great God that my sisters are all good. As to the acts of the community, we take care to neglect nothing».

For this so pleasing letter the Mother rejoices with Sr. A. Fulgenzia and gives her the appropriate advice for the good running of both the community and the hospital.

Hence the marvelous and rapid development of the hospital.

Soon restorations and adaptations became necessary, to finance which it was necessary to appeal to the generosity of the citizens.

All responded with enthusiasm to the appeal and the hospital was enriched with new and airy wards, an operating theatre, a room for X-ray examinations, paying rooms. Later it had a large and comfortable kitchen and a completely isolated ward for tubercular diseases.

Further restorations under way provided it with a modern laundry, a sterilizer, a “patients’ wardrobe” and a ward for infectious diseases. The enlargement of the premises allowed the accommodation of 80 inpatients.

The Agreement was renewed several times, with the due adjustments to the laws in force.

Beginning in 1969, the downsizing of the works became necessary owing to the decrease in members, the decline of vocations, deaths and departures of sisters, even young ones. In this process the hospital of Orbetello was spared for some more years, and the sisters left it on 17.12.1974, not without regret on the part of the Administrators, grateful for the service rendered by the Daughters of Saint Anne and with the hope of a second return (Cf. letter of 19.12.1974).

Linked to the hospital of Orbetello are the names of three sisters who distinguished themselves by merits and virtues.

Sr. Fulgenzia Bocciarelli, (already mentioned), who directed the work for 36 years. A true angel of charity, charitable with all, she faced with utmost courage the dangers of cholera, smallpox and typhus which then raged in Orbetello and the countryside. At the bedside of the sick she forgot food and rest. With good manners, but above all with prayer, she induced even the most recalcitrant to desire the Holy Sacraments. Countless conversions due to her were remembered. She passed away on 29 August 1917 as a result of a cruel disease contracted in the performance of duty. The Congregation of Charity paid her solemn honors and assigned to her body a distinguished place in the Municipal Cemetery.

Sr. A. Emidia Risi held the post of cook for fully 40 years. Always ready for prayer, she was an example of exact observance and sacrifice. Not content with her wearisome daytime work, she too wanted her turn at the night watch. She was a collaborator of the Superior Fulgenzia during the epidemic periods. Worn out by physical toil and become almost blind, she died a holy death on 28 October 1928. The Congregation of Charity wished to perpetuate her memory, having a fine epigraph placed on her tomb.

Sr. A. Annunziata Magnani, an example of humility and prayer, assisted with edifying charity and self-denial in the lazaretto those afflicted with smallpox and typhus. She passed to her eternal reward on 18 June 1939.

(Cf. AFSA Prot. 1881-86 D.4/36; M.4/32; Foundations).

8. SUCRE. HOSPITAL.

In 1882 the third expedition of sisters for Bolivia took place. Sr. A. Camilla Valentini was placed at the head of this large party. She relates that, having to go to the southern part of Bolivia and therefore to cross the most majestic part of the Cordillera of the Andes, she was forced into a difficult, tiring, dangerous journey.

Finally, after months and months of hardship, on 6 August of the same year the religious arrived, tired indeed but happy, at the city of Sucre, then Capital of the Republic. They were guests of the very kind Arce family.

The group was made up of Sr. A. Camilla Valentini (Superior), Sr. A. Immacolata Cavassa, Sr. A. Guida Novelli, Sr. A. Margherita Fantozzi, Sr. A. Agnese Facchini, Sr. A. Damiana Odone, Sr. Giacobba Freichler, Sr. A. Guindalina Campora, Sr. A. Stefania Camia, Sr. A. Cesira Noci, Sr. A. Amalia Fabrini, Sr. A. Nicolina Andreis.

After some days of rest they took lodging in a house owned by Dr. Arce, in the 25 de Mayo square; there they were the object of demonstrations of affection and attentions from the whole citizenry, who felt proud to have the first Religious in their own city. Some time later, when the hospital was in a condition to receive them, they began their humanitarian mission.

On 8 December 1882, after an agreement with the Municipal Authorities, part of the Religious took on the work of the “Santa Barbara” hospital, while the others devoted themselves to teaching at private homes, helping at the same time their hospital-working sisters.

9. VALENZA PO (AL). Hospital – Home for the elderly - 1882.

The hospital-hospice of Valenza Po (AL) was founded in 1832 by Canon Vincenzo Zuffi with his own patrimony and that of Mrs. Teresa Lana. At first it was run by lay people and only fifty years later, that is, in 1882, did the Daughters of Saint Anne take over.

By a resolution of 1 January 1882, passed unanimously, it is decided to entrust the hospital complex to a religious Congregation and preferably to the Daughters of Saint Anne.

The president Lebba makes a formal request to the Superior general, Mother Rosa Gattorno, on 18 January 1882, begging her, when passing through Piedmont, to go in person to that town to visit the hospital, to learn of the healthfulness and pleasantness of the place, to inform herself personally of whatever may be of interest to her, and at the same time to reach a mutual agreement. At the same time he declares himself ready to go to Piacenza to contact her in person.

The Mother replies a few days later, saying that owing to commitments she will not be able to make the visit: “if they are in a hurry it can be arranged by letter, and it will be better for him to come” in the coming month of May.

The meeting takes place on 23 May 1882, the date on which the conditions for stipulating the Agreement are defined.

The sisters (four) arrive in Valenza Po at the end of August 1882. They are: Sr. Chiara Rossi, Sr. A. Cesira Noci, Sr. A. Martiniana Brandi, Sr. A. Remigia Moreni.

Sr. A. Chiara Rossi, a Superior with a little experience behind her, writes to the Mother after four days, revealing to her the reality of the new work.

“We arrived in Alessandria at 2 in the afternoon to continue at 5 for Valenza. The Archbishop showed himself pleased and wanted us to have coffee with him. There was a great celebration with gentlemen, young ladies and all the priests. I would not accept the meal except at the hospital and by ourselves; everyone waited outside the room and meanwhile we ate… I found a fine hospital with 33 chronic patients and then a fine garden, but there is great disorder and great abuses. The filth cannot be described, insects and lice everywhere. It seems impossible that they can be removed, it will take time”.

Rolling up their sleeves, the sisters begin the cleaning, but they need help because there is much work, although there is a male nurse who “trembles all over” and cannot really do much.

Here everyone is content – she continues in the letter of 4 September 1882 – a lady gives us fruit every day.

The Superior senses that the number of sisters must be increased and speaks of it with the commission. Her request is granted and she loses no time in making it known to the Mother. Confidentially and with great freedom, she ventures to suggest a sister who would do well, having hospital experience, who would come willingly because she knows her and was her novitiate companion. Sr. A. Sebastiana is robust – she adds in the letter – used to work in the fields, and could very well be more useful in Valenza than in Florence.

She also assures that she will provide the money for the journey and is ready to send it.

The correspondence follows at a frequent pace. Fine and consoling news reaches Mother Gattorno. Their arrival was a triumph, all are content: the commission, the inhabitants, the old people. They have much work, it is true, but they enjoy a paradise-like peace. She begs the Mother to send “with the sister who will come” the linen, because they lack things.
