We have no – she writes – white caps or skirts to change into, we are down to the “pearls of Saint Anne”.

As for those cared for, Sr. A. Chiara has already arranged for the making of the cloaks; Sr. A. Cesira attends to the laundry and Sr. A. Martiniana to the care of the elderly. The population notices the poverty of the hospital and helps with offerings in kind, pieces of cloth and some small sum.

The Superior does not fail to confess to the Mother her discomfort about the observance of the times for prayers. For now – she says – we do what we can, but everything is observed.

Meanwhile the requested sister has arrived, with whom she is pleased: she is robust, but she would like her to be more gracious and sweeter to content the “poor old men”.

She awaits a visit from the Mother to hear her advice and learn various things concerning the hospital. She affirms once again that the sisters are content, that they work with good will for God and for the Holy Mother, that they all get along, hoping they can continue so in the future.

The hospital has been cleaned; it has become beautiful, but it was difficult to remove the abuses and disorders.

What toil, dear Mother! The worst men of the town we have, and yet, with the grace of the Lord and of the Holy Mother, they are content (Letter of 19.9.82).

Awaiting the Mother’s coming to Valenza, the Superior continues to inform her: “The old men are 30. We are five, but the work is always great. Before we came, the hospital was abandoned, no one wanted to come, now all are fond of it”.

The hospital is in order; the sisters can better observe the times for prayer. On Sundays there are two Masses, attended by the old men, who also recite the rosary, and by outsiders.

The Superior watches not only over the running of the work, but is attentive above all to the spiritual life of the sisters.

I am pleased with the sisters – she writes – our old men are fond of them, I find them content and attached to you, Mother, as also to me. It is known, there is some little fault but one must be forbearing, we are not saints after all, but we have peace. She does not fail, besides, to provide for the sisters, although she dislikes spending: she does not want the sisters to suffer from the cold.

With the passing of time the hospital developed. It was enlarged several times and then replaced so as to be able to accommodate 170 persons, mostly elderly.

Of the sisters the city press said: “They carry out the internal service with admirable self-denial and Christian charity”.

Sr. A. Filomena Menalli, on 30 October 1933, was awarded the gold medal. This presence ceased in June 1981.

The seed of goodness made new vocations germinate, so that the priests themselves directed young women to join the Daughters of Saint Anne.

It is known that Mother Gattorno visited the hospital and stayed there for several days.

Prot. 1881-86: N.89/81 AFSA D.5 Racc.43; M.4 Racc.31

10. COCHABAMBA (BOLIVIA). VIEDMA HOSPITAL.

The Daughters of Saint Anne came to Bolivia in 1878 at the request of the Municipality.

In 1882, at the request of the Municipality, the San Salvador hospital was established in Cochabamba with the sending of eight sisters, among them Sr. A. Cunegonda Conti, superior of the nascent Community.

Nothing had been prepared for the sisters’ residence; they were forced to sleep in the same places where shortly before there had been typhus patients, with almost no prior disinfection, so that three young religious were infected, offering their lives to the Lord.

The small and squalid premises were transformed little by little into a comfortable stay for the unfortunate Indians who for the first time lay down on a straw mattress with sheets.

In 1884 the patients of the old hospital were transferred to the new building called Viedma Hospital: the premises were exchanged for others larger and more comfortable; the “covaccia” (a kind of niche made of sun-baked bricks) was exchanged for an iron bed.

As the number of patients grew, the sisters and the medical staff tripled.

In May 1907 the superior Sr. A. Cunegonda Conti asked for and obtained permission to have a chapel built in the same hospital for the use of the Religious, the patients and the staff: a most beautiful church which, after the Cathedral, is one of the loveliest in the city, where Mother Saint Anne is solemnly venerated.

In 1911 the new church was inaugurated, which proved a great satisfaction.

The sisters, while they served in this Hospital, never weakened their charity, so that the population of Cochabamba venerates the institution of the Daughters of Saint Anne with great gratitude.

11. CANZANO (TE). Kindergarten – Elementary school - 1882.

The president of the Congregation of Charity, Agostino Taraschi, commissioned by Mr. Teodosio Scarselli, who had previously turned to Mother Gattorno, on 14 July 1882 renews the request to entrust to the Daughters of Saint Anne the building left by the Dominican sisters.

Mother Rosa agrees to the request and conclusions are reached, after agreements on both sides.

The Congregation asks for four sisters: two for the kindergarten, one certified for the elementary school (1st and 2nd grades) and the fourth with the task of Superior, to keep the internal order and discipline unchanged and to replace the sisters when they were prevented from carrying out their duties.

The salary amounts to £.1550, equal to that paid to the Dominicans, and in addition £.100 are assigned for wood and coal for heating the classrooms.

The petitioner alludes to the need for persons who unite to the spirit of charity those requirements indispensable to anyone called to educate and instruct boys and girls of every class. The sisters are expected for 1 September, but the Foundress confirms their arrival for 4 October 1882, just the time needed for the choice of persons.

The President insists on the recommendation that the documentation qualifying for teaching conform to the laws of the Provincial School Council, so that no obstacles to approval are met (Letter of 10.09.1882).

On the 4th, punctually, the sisters arrive in Canzano. They are:

Sr. A. Berarda Cattani (Superior)

Sr. A. Ermenegilda Mostardini (teacher)

Sr. A. Evangelista Bigonti (teacher)

Sr. A. Fedele Ducci (teacher)

The President’s letter is dated the following day, in which he thanks the Mother, hoping that with the presence of the sisters and with God’s help the town will see its expectations crowned. “There is great satisfaction – he writes – in every respect and it is not feared that this course will later change. All are animated by a strong resolve to fulfil their holy mission and the Superior is rich not only in every merit, but has an uncommon prudence and graciousness”.

Sr. A. Berarda Cattani, at the same time, informs the Mother Foundress of their arrival, at two after midnight. The journey was most happy, but at that nighttime hour the President who was to be at the station was not seen until ten.

Before settling in the new house, they are accompanied to the bishop’s palace. The bishop of Teramo welcomes them fatherly and says he is pleased with their presence, “he likes the habit immensely”, and expresses the wish to meet their Mother Foundress and to see her soon.

Thus the Superior continues in the letter of 5 October: “Here at Canzano we arrived at 3 in the afternoon. The President had the meal prepared for us; he had the patience to show us everything everywhere, all the corners where to put our things, and the next day we were presented to the Administration. How good everyone is, my Mother! Here, if we wish, we can do every good, because I have understood that they are all good Christians and that they expect “serious” sisters, with decorum as is due, religious”.

The people are very pleased with the Daughters of Saint Anne and await a fifth sister in help. On 29 October, in fact, Sr. A. Barbiana Carbonini arrives, whom the President describes as “delightful, wise and prudent”.

The correspondence exchanged is dense with news. All goes well as regards the school, providence has not been lacking; they have given the sum of £.390 for three months, with which the Superior will buy a little wheat, beans and potatoes for the winter, hoping also to save a little. The pupils increase day by day, there are 36 and there is much to do.

The sisters are all well, they are good – she writes – and peace is always among us; this is my first prayer at the start of the day. Dear Mother, one thing we lack here, which is the most important: for now there is no Blessed Sacrament, but the president gave me good hopes” (Letter of 14.10.1882).

The Mother replies encouraging her daughters, who thank her for the warnings and counsels and promise to be observant of the holy Rules, so that by their example they may be a consolation to her heart (Letter of 12.11.1882).

The school was establishing itself; it was esteemed both in the town and in the surrounding areas, so that pupils from Giulianova and Teramo were added.

The expansion of the Institute and the opening of new houses often led Mother Gattorno to transfer personnel, something not very welcome to the Administrators. The school was under the supervision of the Provincial Authorities, inspections were frequent and everything had to be according to the norms. It was not always possible to comply with the laws and for this reason Mother Benedetta Carrega, already from 1907, began to think of withdrawing the Sisters.

The failure to take part in the Competition, announced by the Provincial Council for the appointment of teachers, was the final cause for leaving the school of Canzano, in August 1912.

12. CASSANO DELLE MURGE (BA). Kindergarten - 1882.

9 May 1882 marks the date of the request for the Sisters Daughters of Saint Anne to take on the teaching in the municipal Kindergarten of Cassano delle Murge. It is the director Giuseppe D’Alessandro who turns to Mother Rosa to obtain three teachers, adding the contractual conditions:

the kindergarten will open on 2 November 1882;

the Institute is offered decent lodging;

the salary will be in line with what sisters usually receive, besides domestic help, fuel, lighting and the furnishing of the house limited to what is necessary;

some travel allowance if strictly required.

It is further foreseen that in the first months of 1883 the new hospital for the poor sick will open, the care of which is established to be entrusted to the same sisters. In that case the number of sisters would rise to four.

The same request is supported by the mayor, Gaetano Perotti, who expresses “his ardent wish that the matter be concluded as soon as possible” (Letter of 16 May 1882).

Mother Rosa replies on the 21st of the same month; she accepts the conditions and proposes a fourth sister, who will be able to enjoy all that is granted to the others, except the salary and travel allowance. Further correspondence follows, by which the conditions and the date of arrival are defined.

The sisters are expected on 1 November 1882. “They will have to take the Bologna-Ancona-Bari line, where, there being a connection with the train on the Taranto line, they will take their seats on it as far as the station of Acquaviva delle Fonti, from which they will be collected by a representative of the Commission”.

Having arrived at Cassano: Sr. A. del Carmelo Vacherini, Sr. A. Emerenziana Bossi, Sr. A. Eufemia Ruggeri and Sr. A. Eufrasia Cervi receive a most beautiful welcome.

“The children are over 100, boys and girls – writes the Superior Vacherini – another sister is needed. The one you send me must be educated because there is much to work, since the children are many. We, except Sr. A. Emerenziana, who has a cough, are all well”.

The Superior has no clock and cannot sound the wake-up; so she asks the mother for one, who could send it with the sister who will come or give her permission to buy it. In the report she continues with other considerations. Sr. A. Emerenziana, to tell the truth, lacks the due preparation, and to Sr. A. Del Carmelo, very shrewd, she entrusts the children for some hours in her absence, maintaining before the Administrators of the Kindergarten that the aforesaid is a nurse and probably will not stay. Meanwhile she herself is not well either and is forced to bed for a week (Letter of 24.11.82).

The construction works of the new hospital proceed. It is intended to use the first floor for the kindergarten, but because of dampness this is postponed and it will take at least three years. The sisters are dissatisfied. ”The children are many; the house is cramped and we suffer not a little – the superior writes to the Foundress – one fell and hurt his head; it is almost a month and he is still ill, the doctor comes twice a day to dress it. I beg you to commend him to God that he may recover sooner; I am so distressed” (Letter of 20.4.1885).

Within a few months the situation worsened completely. The change of some sisters for health or other reasons, without due notice and especially during the current year, had unleashed discontent in the Commission. The Director himself, who had asked for their presence, now shows all his hostility. Salaries are not paid and the sisters are often mortified, despised and mocked even by outsiders.

The outpourings, sufferings and humiliations of her daughters reached the Mother’s heart, who could not but take note of the inconveniences that had arisen. What could the remedy be? To withdraw the sisters. The danger was averted, but only for a few months. The momentary return, so earnestly implored, of the former superior Placida made it possible for the examinations to be given and that thorny affair to be concluded. The President, with a letter dated 12 July 1885, communicated that in the following August the sisters “would be free”, while remaining for some months in Cassano at their pleasure, but that in the coming school year 1885-86 the kindergarten would pass into the hands of the new teachers.

For her part, on 24 July 1885, Sr. A. Marina, the new superior, notified the Mother that the Commission had provided the sum for the return journey from Cassano to Piacenza. With her would leave Sr. A. Marca and Sr. A. Davidina.

(Cf. AFSA Prot. 1881-86 D.7/58; M.5/33; Foundations).

13. ZIBELLO (PR). “DAGNINI” HOSPITAL 1882.

The initiatives for the settlement of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Zibello begin on 22 March 1882. The request is made by the Mayor as president of the hospital.

In April the members of the Commission meet Mother Rosa Gattorno and agree everything in person. On 18 April the Foundress sends as an example the contract with the hospital of Busseto, with a note of what is needed for the sisters, who were to be four: three paid, the fourth would be paid from 1884 (cf. Protocol 1881-1886, autograph of the Foundress).

It is agreed, however, that the sisters will arrive in Zibello on 11 November 1882, a date absolutely respected.

The Superior is Sr. A. Ermanna Fantozzi, in charge of the accounts and running of the hospital; collaborators: Sr. A. Fabrizia Intropida, cook, and Sr. A. Rosolina Emasi, wardrobe keeper and care of the sick.

In 1983, at the centenary commemoration, a plaque was placed at the entrance of the house, expressing recognition and gratitude to the Sisters. One of them, Sr. A. Graziella Pompei, on the same date was awarded a gold medal for having given the work 40 years of admirable service.

Over the 124 years of the Daughters of Saint Anne’s presence in Zibello, despite the changes of personnel, there were always serene relations with the Administrators for the good running of the Institution. The Agreement was renewed several times to make the necessary adjustments.

On 22 October 2006 the Sisters ended their service, leaving the luminous trail of their exemplary self-giving and much nostalgia in those who benefited from their loving services, imbued with evangelical charity.

(Cf. AFSA Prot. 1881-1886; D. 5/36)

14. COMAZZO (MI). Orphanage for children of both sexes – Women’s workshop 1882.

The priest Don Luigi Mazzola, parish priest of Comazzo, having at heart the education and instruction of children of both sexes and of the young women, took an interest in having the sisters in his small town, after hearing that the Dominican Tertiary sisters of Casolate were leaving the workshop run by them.

He asked the support of Canon Paolo Gagliardi, of the diocese of Lodi, who, being on good terms with the Superior general of the Daughters of Saint Anne, could better exert influence to obtain three sisters in Comazzo. To this end, the good priest also informed the Marquises Durazzo, who, sensitive to the advancement of the girls, who were rather devoted to field work, were glad to be able to continue the work.

Negotiations begin. Don Luigi writes to Mother Gattorno stating the conditions. “They will have an annual salary of £ 935, besides wood in the winter period to heat the classrooms, in one of which are gathered the boys and girls not younger than three nor older than seven; and in the other the girls and young women who attend the retreat, or wish to take part in it when they are not in the fields. There is a plot with vines and fruit trees from which the Sisters can draw vegetables for the whole year, being of sufficient size. The premises are all on the upper floor, in the best position in the town. They consist of two rooms for the girls, two dormitories and a small room for the nuns, besides a small reception room, a little oratory, the kitchen, a small adjoining storeroom” (Letter of 21.08.1882).

The sisters will have to take care of teaching Christian doctrine, impart the rudiments of reading and writing and look after the girls in women’s crafts.

On 1 November 1882 the contract is signed.

The Mother General accepts the conditions improved by the brother Marquises Giacomo and Agostino – the annual salary will be £. 1,100, payable in cash and quarterly – and promises that on Saturday 25 November 1882 she will send the three sisters.

The Superior is Sr. A. Filiberta Bertuzzi, accompanied by Sr. A. della Natività Rapillo and Sr. A. Enrichetta.

A few days after the settlement, the Marquis Giacomo Durazzo writes to the Mother general with satisfaction and gratitude. “I cannot express to you – he says – the contentment we feel at seeing the impulse of Christian charity, joined to profound humility, with which they set to work at once to obtain the greater glory of God by directing to Him the souls of the poor little ones. They paid no heed to the hundred things that were lacking in a newly established house and only sought to get to know at once the girls and children entrusted to their care” (Letter of 28.11.1882).

Some months pass and, for her part, Sr. A. Filiberta reports to Mother Gattorno on how the house is going. The first difficulties arise and she informs her of the situation: they lack the necessary linen; the chapel lacks what is needed, the Bishop does not allow them to have the Most Blessed Sacrament and they necessarily must attend the parish Mass, there being only one priest, so that they cannot observe the community timetable exactly.

The Parish Priest, however, says he is well disposed to meet them in any need.

Beyond all this, the Superior again expresses her regret and the worry of having to provide what is lacking and appeals to the charity of the Mother, who, sensitive to her daughters’ needs, provides with solicitude for the nascent community (letter of 2.2.1883).

The Superior, writing to her, thanks her and adds that the Marquis is pleased with their work, that he has already provided some things they lacked and that he will soon visit the sisters with his family and then draw up the inventory.

The workshop is well attended: the girls number 40, as do “the little ones”. The Sunday oratory teems with boys and the work is great. The sisters are well liked, they obtain approval on all sides, but the poor health of two sisters begins to pose problems and to undermine the stability of the Community. Certified sisters are requested for teaching. Mother Rosa temporizes; unable to respond adequately, in June 1887 she decides to withdraw the sisters from Comazzo.

AFSA Prot. 1881-86: 335/81; D.5 Racc.43; M.4 Racc.31

15. BITONTO (BA). Poorhouse 1882.

On 23 May 1868, in the former Capuchin convent, the “Prince Umberto” Poorhouse was founded on the initiative of a Charitable Society of Bitonto.

After some decades, by resolution of the Governing Council, presided over by the canon theologian Gaetano Valenti, it was determined to entrust the direction of the Poorhouse “to the Honorable Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne”, after the agreements that had been reached. The convention lasted five years from 1 November 1882.

The Foundress undertook to send three sisters, one of whom, in the opinion of the Governing Council, could take over the direction of the “Princess Margherita” Kindergarten and live with the others. If the Mother then wished to send a fourth sister, she would be at her own expense.

The annual salary amounted to £. 450 with oil and coal; the dwelling, provided with all that was needed, plus travel expenses, for the first time only.

The religious arrived at Bitonto on 31 October 1882 with an advance telegram sent by Mother Rosa.

Sr. A. Egea Codeghini, designated as Superior, has the task of the accounts and is very attentive to saving; the others, Sr. A. Domenica and Sr. A. Pacifica, are assigned to care for the 25 residents of both sexes.

“I feel great regret – writes the Superior – that in this house I cannot observe silence because, dealing with these poor people, I have to raise my voice; now, moreover, we have a deaf-mute… sick, chronic patients… Patience is needed, one must work for our Jesus who suffered so much for us. We are all well and content. In these two months I have made a little saving and I send you 50 lire. Forgive me, dear Mother, if it is little; I make the bread at home and for this too I have found much saving” (Letter of 22.12.1882).

Mother Rosa informs her that she will go to Bitonto by way of Bari. Sr. A. Egea, who already knows the route, advises her to reach the station of Santo Spirito, which is an hour from Bitonto, and will arrange to send her the carriage (Letter of 31.12.1882).

With a letter of 13.02.83 she informs the Mother of the death of a sister, the honors received… the accompaniment to the cemetery by 50 priests, all with a torch in hand… the singular privilege of having been buried in the tomb of the cloistered nuns.

From the dense correspondence of Sr. A. Egea we know that many young women asked to join the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne; she was very careful in sifting vocations, using the information of their respective confessors.

The work developed over time. In 1905 a distinguished benefactress, Mrs. Griffi, had a pavilion built from scratch to house the residents with greater hygiene; in 1911 another benefactor, Mr. Giuseppe Ventafridda, donated a second pavilion, which was used as a “Little hospital for chronic patients” for women only.

Subsequently the work underwent progressive and continual improvements, in economic, building and health terms alike, and the name of the home was changed to “Villa Giovanni XXIII – Home for the elderly”.

The sisters’ service always won the applause of the ecclesiastical and civil Authorities, as well as that of the citizenry; they made the environment welcoming and comfortable for so many people tried by poverty, loneliness, illness and other sufferings.

The strong moments of reflection and prayer were marked by the calendar of popular devotions, such as the Marian month, the month of the Sacred Heart and the various novenas. The public church attached to the house was a lively center of evangelization through catechesis, liturgy and fraternal dialogue (see Rel. 1964).

The work was carried on by the Daughters of Saint Anne until 30 June 1995. The shortage of lay staff and the advanced age of the sisters, who were also subjected to substitute work beyond their strength, did not allow their presence to continue at Villa Giovanni XXIII. Expressions of gratitude were made by the Board to the five sisters leaving the Home, for the long service which the Daughters of Saint Anne, succeeding one another for over 100 years, rendered in Bitonto.

(Cf. AFSA Prot. 1881-86 D.4/45; M.5/33; Foundations).

16. ACCADIA (FG). Municipal Elementary School - 1881.

The mayor Antonio Vassalli had commissioned, about six months earlier, the bishop of Bovino to work to obtain the sisters for teaching in the elementary schools of Accadia. The lay teachers had been dismissed and it was chosen to bring in religious. This first request was followed by that of the Mayor, dated 28 November 1881, in which he begged the Mother to send three sisters: “one holding a higher-grade certificate and two of a lower grade and, if possible, a fourth for company and assistance”. Mother Rosa, not having the religious requested, replied a few days later that it was impossible for that year and that “if they will wait, it will be for next year”.

Mr. Vassalli assured the Mother that the sisters would be well received both by the Administration and by the citizenry.

“The premises – he writes – are excellent both for dwelling and for the schools, the air is good, the water also; the Municipality does not lack what is needed for life and there are means of transport and other conveniences”. The mayor, with simplicity and also with familiarity, advises the Mother that “if she cannot immediately dispose of the personnel for setting up the new house she can take them from Bovino and send novices there”.

On 9 September 1882, Mother Rosa communicates two names: Sr. A. Luigia and Sr. A. Lucilla, for approval, but lets some months pass for the final decisions.

The sisters arrive in Accadia on 20 December 1882.

On the 22nd, Sr. A. Stefanina Marchetti tells Mother Rosa she is happy to find herself in a truly observant community. “I have been here two days. Oh, what fine lessons these sisters gave me, of silence and of every sort of regular observance”.

Most consoling is the report of the superior, Sr. A. Zenobia della Valle, whose letter bears the date of 25 December. She writes thus: “Having arrived at Bovino (a neighboring town where the Daughters of Saint Anne already resided), we were kindly welcomed by the Bishop, awaiting the Mayor’s arrangements. The next day we reach Accadia, where part of the people were waiting before the door”.

For the moment they live in a different (rented) house, waiting for their dwelling to be ready and provided with everything. The Mayor, in fact, instructs the Superior to go to Naples with another sister to buy everything needed for the house.

Sr. A. Zenobia does nothing but extol the goodness and kindness of the Mayor, as well as of his mother, who provides the sisters with food.

“What a good family! Two girls come to our school. They are very well-mannered… Dear Mother – the superior continues – what toil to educate the girls! They are so ill-bred that they inspire compassion; they are so undisciplined that they give not a moment’s respite, much more mine who are the worst, being older. May Jesus think of it and Saint Anne do Herself all that I must do, because I find myself tangled like chicks in tow”. What simplicity and what trust in this letter!

In another letter, dated 23 March 1883, she gives news of the sisters’ health. Sr. A. Stefanina Marcotti has a cough and this is due to the house being damp; she spoke of it to the Mayor, who immediately provided two sacks of coal to keep the fire lit.

For his part, the Mayor Vassalli abounds in praise of the sisters. I feel it my duty – he writes to the Foundress – to keep you informed of the good outcome of these Schools… of my satisfaction and that of this Administration with the way the said Schools have been run by the present Teachers and with their behavior in general… here they have been well received by the public” (Letter of 9 August 1883).

The subsequent correspondence continues in the same tone of satisfaction: “Of the sisters who dwelt and of those who are at present in Accadia I tell you briefly: in everything they are to be praised, both in themselves and for the moral, religious and instructive good brought to the women and therefore to the families of Accadia. Of the Superior Zenobia… I say: with the sisters, with the pupils, with everyone she is amiable, assiduous, diligent, endowed with great sagacity…

All enjoy excellent repute with this clergy, the Municipality itself, private families and the people (Letter of the Archpriest Michelangelo Raffa to the Mother).

Good, unfortunately, is fought. Indeed, after some years envies, calumnies and hostilities began to creep in against the sisters. Sr. A. Zenobia left Accadia in 1889.

“Here we work and suffer, writes Sr. A. di S. Giuseppe Morelli – but all for the glory of God; the day will come when our enemies will yield and we hope it is not far off” (Letter of 20.10.1905).

This sister, Sr. A. Stefanina Marchetti and Sr. A. Scolastica D’Aniello, not without suffering, after some years, because of hostility from teachers who aspired to the jobs held by the sisters, had to leave the town in 1907, to the deep regret of the mayor Vassalli and of the clergy who had affectionately taken up their defense.

(Cf. AFSA Prot. 1881-86 D.4/37; M.4/33; F. 5/49 Foundations).

17. SIENA. NURSES’ HOUSE.

On 1 April 1882, the Rev. Fr. Gaetano Gesti, Archiepiscopal Secretary, began negotiations with Mother Gattorno to establish in Siena a Community of Daughters of Saint Anne as nurses and, for this purpose, offered to the Institute as property the house that the Sisters would inhabit.

Mother Rosa, ready to enlarge her heart and expand it in charity at every opportunity God presented to her, accepted and, on 8 December of that same year, eight sisters opened the new house.

Festive was the welcome given to the religious, as recounted by Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi, superior of the nascent work. A detailed description of the beginnings highlights how much the sisters were esteemed, honored and helped by the Archbishop who had wanted them in his Diocese (Cf. Letters of Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi 1882).

The sick grew in number day by day and the sisters took turns in caring for them, day and night. They lived in poverty and on alms-collecting twice a week, until they had generous benefactors.

The Mother rejoiced at her daughters’ work and did not fail to console also the heart of Sr. Anna Crocifissa, saying she was very glad that all was going well and thanking God for it (cf. Letter of 23.12.1882). And take care also that the sisters do not lack what is necessary, indeed that you pay particular attention to Sr. A. Amante la Barbera... By obedience I want Sr. A. Amante to eat meat, steaks every day with boiled beef, and also two good glasses of generous wine, one at lunch and the other at supper. (Letter of 2.12.83)

In 1920, meeting a real need of many young students, the sisters, under the direction of the superior Sr. A. Maurina Moise, entered another field of action, establishing a boarding house that immediately developed widely.

Restored with modern criteria and provided with all the required amenities, the house of Siena offered 50 beds for boarders and young university women.

In 1984 it became a residence for the elderly sisters and in 1998 it was definitively closed, and the premises put to other uses.

AFSA Prot.1881-86 F.5.41

18. PUTIGNANO. Civil Hospital “S. Maria degli Angeli” -1882.

It was founded in 1600 by the Noble Lady Francesca Antoniano, assisted by the Confraternity of “Death and Prayer”, based in the former Dominican convent.

The first document, from which we learn of the interest of Mr. Vincenzo Laterza, president of the Pious Work, who was getting ready to finish the premises for the settlement of the Community of the Daughters of Saint Anne, dates from 12 September 1882.

The Bishop of Conversano, on 21 September, being on pastoral Visitation in Putignano, interceded in his turn, because of those same sisters, already present in his Diocese, “the qualities and virtues with which they were adorned were well known”.

President Laterza’s keen interest meant that by 25 September the premises were already ready and the Foundress could arrange to send the sisters before the end of the month. He also gave directions for the journey, suggesting they reach the nearby station of Polignano a Mare, where they would be met by the Administration.

Mother Rosa, for her part, confirmed from Piacenza, on 24 September, that she had accepted the terms for the introduction of the Daughters of Saint Anne into the hospital “S. Maria degli Angeli”. This letter was answered by the President with expressions of infinite gratitude, of most special thanks, deeming the assignment of such sisters “a most singular favor” […] a fortunate acceptance on the part of this Pious Society which, despite the scarcity of members, had found a way to satisfy him”.

According to the contract, the same as for other similar institutions, the presence of four religious was foreseen, with particular care “that one should be suited to dispensing medicines; the medicines, in fact, were administered at home, since the hospital could not receive all the sick and was equipped with a mediocre pharmacy”.

Now a further notice is awaited for the sisters’ coming; delay suits the petitioner too, so that everything may be well prepared to receive them. On 9 December he sends the sum of £. 300 for the journey, repeating the plea that one of them have those pharmaceutical qualifications with which the Superior of Rutigliano (Sr. A. Assunta Saccani) is endowed.

The sisters: Sr. A. Vittoria Archetti, Sr. A. dell’Ascensione and Sr. A. Marcella Barosi arrive at Polignano a Mare at 3:45 in the afternoon, met by the Commission as agreed. Among them, unfortunately, is not the much-desired pharmacist, for whom the Mother will provide in May 1883. They are lodged in an apartment of three beautiful rooms used as a dormitory, a dining room, the kitchen and two other rooms for the direction, where to spend free and leisure hours.

Meanwhile, for some time the Superior of Rutigliano is with them, trying to get the sisters started; they show all good will to learn how medicines are dispensed.

Sr. A. Silvestrina Perrot, expert in pharmacy, as had been promised, joins the others. She comes from the Hospital of Naples and, having a little more experience, at once gives the idea of a sister adequately prepared and sure of herself. It sometimes happens, however, that intelligence and charity are not always in perfect harmony. Despite the exhortations of the Superior Archetti, there is no harmony among the sisters in understanding and attention toward the latest arrival (of a character – we might say – discontented, closed and solitary): the pharmacist, perhaps a little jealous of her knowledge, does not like to pass it on… It is clear that a climate of discontent can be felt, and not only inside, which afflicts the Superior, to the point of wishing to leave her post and go to America (which will happen in 1884, leaving for Brazil).

The situation becomes so tense that the Foundress Mother intervenes by changing the pharmacist, and once again it is Sr. A. Assunta Saccani who hastens to the rescue. She will do so for a short time, until the arrival of Sr. A. Aquilina Gilardoni, an excellent sister who, besides her training, has a strong and well-formed spirit and knows how to unite her knowledge with the “wisdom of the heart”. The renewed community lives in joy and peace. The communications to the Mother are consoling, also on the part of the Administrators, who, amazed, ask Sr. A. Aquilina where she attended the pharmacy courses.

As has been said before, the replacement of sisters happened very frequently: sometimes for internal reasons, sometimes at the will of the President of the work, who demanded healthy, robust, suitable, capable religious… A series of changes follows, in fact, to establish balance above all with the Directors.

From 28 April 1891 is the letter of Fr. Giovanni Guarnieri, internal Director of the hospital, who writes thus to Mother Rosa: “[…] I speak to you first of all of the local superior (Sr. A. Cleta Sartori), who will personally hand you this letter, of whom I can only proclaim her excellent moral qualities. She scrupulously fulfills her duties and conscientiously carries out her office, being loving with everyone and attentive to all that concerns the good running of this hospital. I am exceedingly pleased, as is the whole Commission, and can only thank you […]. There is Sr. A. Raimondina, who with the utmost precision carries out the office of Pharmacist entrusted to her, and is so exact as to reach scrupulosity. Sr. A. Davidina is excellent in the arduous office of cook, all the more because she manages it being of robust health. The very good and shy Sr. A. Oliva fulfills with care and diligence the assistance of the Wards; and though of frail health, she is now well and it is hoped she will acquire perfect health.

Sr. A. Predicanda too has shown herself a good and diligent nurse […]. I can only be pleased with all of them, above all for the great harmony and affection that reign between Superior and subordinates and among the subordinates themselves”.

Besides the hospital, the Daughters of Saint Anne looked after the Kindergarten (from 1892…), the Rest home (1906), the “S. Maria degli Angeli” Conservatory for minors, adjoining the hospital (1909). The influx of patients required successive enlargements, until the hospital was transferred in 1958 to Via Cappuccini, where up to 200 sick people could be received.

From this period dates the advance notice of the Community’s withdrawal, because the number of sisters proved insufficient for the needs of the new wards of pediatrics and of ophthalmology – ENT; nor could others be added for lack of specifically trained sisters. Subsequently, in 1962, the religious staff was reduced and on 3 October 1974 the sisters definitively left the hospital of Putignano.

The following year the president Avv. De Miccolis Angelini wrote thus to the Mother General: “[…] The painful impression at the suppression of that Community… a year after that measure, has not lessened, but rather has grown, because Administrators, medical staff and population have been able to see how many beneficial effects have vanished from the daily life of the Hospital through the absence of the Sisters… Making myself the interpreter of a deeply felt and widespread state of mind, I address a heartfelt plea that… they be willing to study concretely the possibility of rebuilding the Community” (Putignano, 12 June 1975).

AFSA Prot. 1881-1886; D.6/46; M.5/33 Foundations

19. COCHABAMBA (Bolivia). School.

The first to feel the need for the foundation of a house of charity devoted to the education of orphan girls was Dr. Melchor Urquidi. To this end, in the year 1862 he asked for and obtained from the government of Arce a subsidy of 4,000 Bolivian pesos; then, with the voluntary subscription of some neighbors, he was able to set up a modest dwelling in the convent of San Domingo, to which he gave the name “House of the Sisters of Charity”.

Afterward the generous Archdeacon Dr. Manuel Maria Montaño, wishing to develop this work and give it an independent organization, decided to leave his house and some property in favor of poor children, but, since that house did not offer the necessary conditions, he sold it and, under the paternal direction of the most worthy Bishop Francesco Maria del Granado, in the year 1882 the present building in Calle Sucre was bought, to which an embryonic organization was given with the name “School of the Daughters of Mary”, the direction of which was entrusted to the Daughters of Saint Anne.

It was the only institution of religious instruction in this city and was kept going with great difficulty for lack of means.

From the year 1905, thanks to the intelligent direction of the most worthy Superior Sr. A. Amabile Montanari, the School began to show significant development, both in architectural structure and in technical organization: it was equipped with spacious and hygienic dormitories, with a beautiful church in Gothic style, decorated on her own exclusive initiative with true art, so as to be one of the most elegant buildings adorning the city; it had a superb, architecturally modern gymnasium, in which the pupils found the opportunity to cultivate their own artistic gifts, in the fine arts as well as in the useful arts.

For this construction the venerated Mother counted on nothing but the private offerings of well-intentioned people and the savings from the work of each of the admirable religious of the Community who ran the School at their own expense.

At present the school has a modern infrastructure where the Daughters of Saint Anne continue to respond to today’s challenges, working for the integral formation of the new generations of families and educators; a formation founded on Christian values that continues to bring fruits of quality, humanity and solidarity to society and to the Church.

20. PALERMO. “Santo Spirito” Hospital 1883.

In 1883 the “Santo Spirito” hospital is recorded among the foundations in Palermo. This is gathered from a protocol of the time written in Mother Rosa’s own hand, at no. 104; it is recorded that on 15.3.1883 the sisters would have taken up service in that work and would be paid £. 30 each, plus board and an annual habit.

(Cf. List: Houses of the Institute 1866-1939)

21. FRATTAMAGGIORE (NA). Civic Hospital - 1883.

The Daughters of Saint Anne had opened themselves to charity in the Campania region with the establishment of a House in Naples in 1877 and another in Giugliano (NA) in 1881.

Esteem for the new Congregation resounded in the neighboring towns, so that requests for new foundations reached Piacenza, to the heart of Rosa Gattorno, who, having weighed the conditions, almost always answered positively.

It is Cav. Sossio Russo who, on 28.03.1882, turns to the Foundress to obtain three sisters for the Civic Hospital of Frattamaggiore, a hospital with barely 15 beds.

The sisters are asked for a complete service: administration, infirmary, menial service and other duties, except those needed for the male patients, which are not consonant with modesty.

The sisters: Sr. A. Policarpa Alessandrini, Sr. A. Mistica and Sr. Elisea Alessandri arrive in Frattamaggiore on 03 April 1883.

Two days after the arrival, the Superior Sr. A. Policarpa Alessandrini recounts in a letter the festive welcome of the population. Holy Mass is celebrated with numerous priests present, solemnly, “sung”, and at the moment of the elevation the bangs of firecrackers are heard as a sign of celebration. Through an inner entrance from the sacristy they reach the fine premises of the hospital, which stands “solitary” in the wide expanse. There are even armed guards keeping watch, to avoid confusion.

The Superior, who looks after the administration, immediately notices the hospital’s financial straits. For the daily expenses they give her the money, which is often not enough to cover the need.

In the first days, because of the settling in, they have no time to pray. “Without communion – writes Sr. A. Policarpa – I feel as if I were without life. Here things are going quite well, indeed there is nothing bad, but from what I can understand it is a very critical town. I have provided new shoes for everyone because they had none; those they had were all broken and then I had the old ones mended…” (Letter of 05.04.1883).

The tone is no different with which, on 02 November 1883, Sr. A. Peppina Colombini, the Superior who took over the Work a few months later, communicates with the Mother: “The news is good, the administrators are content because the townspeople are very satisfied with what we do for the poor sick; the sick too speak well of us to those who come to visit them. The Mayor, who visited the Hospital, expressed his pleasure at the order and cleanliness”.

The same Superior encourages the sisters and educates them by example to generosity. Indeed, she is the first and does not shrink from the lowest services, counting herself fortunate to serve the sick.

The nascent work is poor in financial means and only God knows the hardships, deprivations and privations to which the sisters are subject. They, however, embrace such poverty with true joy of spirit, glad to spend themselves without measure to relieve others’ misery, to care for souls and bodies, desiring only to bring souls to the Lord!

The health conditions of the town several times put their heroic charity and self-denial to a hard test, not only because of the habitual influx of patients (from the beginning, the patients exceed the foreseen number, hovering around twenty), but also in the two cholera epidemics of 1886/87 and 1910, during which they also served at the Lazaretto, earning praise and blessings.

On 09 December 1888, in some premises adjoining the Hospital, restored and enlarged for the purpose, the poorhouse was inaugurated and another sister was requested.

For this other work the sisters had to provide for the direction of the internal services, the care of the residents, the laundry, the making of the linen and of the clothing needed by them.

That being so, there is no need to go into detail to understand what further sum of sacrifices was asked of them, all the more so as, within a few years, the number of residents rose to 34.

The institution, meanwhile, despite the hardships, was developing, so that, besides increasing the places established in both branches, in 1909 a paying Surgery Section was set up in the Hospital.

The wise, careful and energetic administration of the Sisters had brought the institution to a state of prosperity and had also allowed some restoration work. Thus in 1915, when the European War broke out, the Hospital could be used as a Military Reserve Hospital.

For the occasion, the old people of the Poorhouse were transferred, with the sisters in charge, to the premises of the Schools, and their places were taken by numerous war wounded, who found in our sisters that delicacy of manner and care, that maternal understanding which their distant families could not give them.

Many sisters succeeded one another in the 90 years of presence in the Hospital of Frattamaggiore.

As happened with other works, this Hospital too, in 1974, came within the plan for scaling down activities.

Many appeals were made also by the Administrators, by influential persons and by Religious Authorities, among them Mons. Antonio Cece, bishop of Aversa, and Mons. Agostino Mayer, Secretary of the S. Congregation for Religious, to prevent the sisters’ departure. But the repeated insistence and pressure were firmly rejected, precisely because of the grave shortage of members.

With a letter of 18 January 1971, the Generalate announced the termination of the Agreement and the consequent withdrawal of the religious Community, which took place on 31.12.1974.

22. PIEVE S. STEFANO (AR). Municipal schools - Boarding school - Kindergarten -1883.

A leading figure is Mons. Giustino, Bishop of S. Sepolcro. Having heard from the Daughters of Saint Anne themselves that it was possible to open houses in the territory of his Diocese, prompted by a benefactor, Cav. Nicola Cherici – who put at their disposal a large building (a convent suppressed in Napoleon’s time) for a school with a boarding department – he made the request to Mother Rosa Gattorno.

The Municipality had opened a small hospital there and wished to entrust it to sisters of some pious Institute.

The situation, however, was by no means prosperous. “There are no allowances – we read in the Bishop’s letter, dated 5 June 1882 – it is hoped that the subsistence of the religious can be provided for with some allowance from the Municipality and some subscriptions from private persons and alms. The boarding school and the private school too could serve as help to the new institution”.

The Municipality is well disposed to appoint the religious to the municipal school, so the Bishop recommends to Mother Rosa to send the documents in time to comply with school regulations.

A dense correspondence develops over several months and an agreement is reached in April 1883. Two sisters sent by Mother Rosa make an inspection: they visit the premises to adapt them to the community’s needs and suggest which furnishings to prepare. The Bishop himself promises that, if necessary, together with the Landucci family (benefactors), he will see to the indispensable rest, until the Municipality fixes an allowance.

The opening of the school is set for 29 April, a Sunday. It is good for the sisters to arrive a few days earlier. A four-seat carriage will carry the sisters to S. Sepolcro; on Saturday night they will lodge at the bishop’s residence and the next day, accompanied by the Bishop himself, they will reach Pieve S. Stefano.

Mother Rosa replies on 20 April 1883, saying that they will be notified by telegram of their arrival in Arezzo and that, if there should be any difficulty, it will be communicated in time.

The sisters assigned are: Sr. A. Ferma Cei, Sr. A. Pellegrina, Sr. A. Lazzara. Sr. A. Cristofora.

Sr. A. Ferma (superior) gives the first news to the Foundress Mother on 4 May 1883. The sisters have been received with great contentment, are respected and lack nothing. The people provide for their upkeep; one brings one thing, another another. Mr. Giuseppe Landucci provided the clock… This news is confirmed also by Sr. A. Cristofora, who writes thus on 17.05.1883: “So great is the joy of finding myself in this house, because everyone is fond of us… Everyone vies to come and visit us. What grieves me is to hear that a part are opposed, would not want us… We, thank God, are well and eat with great appetite because the air is so healthy and brings it on. For now we have 50 girls, a little lively, but we hope, with God’s help and that of our mother St. Anne, to make them docile…”.

In another letter of hers, however, we read a touch of discouragement: “There are two parties… At certain moments I find myself a little troubled, having some girls who do not want to hear of going to church and another poor one who has almost one foot in hell. For charity’s sake, dear Mother, pray that the Lord may give me strength to be able to lead them to Him”.

Sr. A. Cristofora teaches in the morning at the municipal school and in the afternoon at the private school, attended by girls from well-off families, set up on the sisters’ own account. The new Superior, Sr. A. Emilia Di Vincenzo, who replaced the first, teaches in the needlework school. Writing to the Mother she gives more consoling news. The Bishop is very pleased, wants the boarding school to be opened and the masons are already at work arranging the premises. The monthly fee will be 30 and 35 lire with the teaching of music and French. Several ladies are already willing to send their little daughters. The benefactors are very pleased… the town shows them many kindnesses. The storms have passed and those who were opposed are now the most respectful. “Mother – she continues in the letter of 20 October 1883 – one must caress them and treat them with kindness… they promise much and then little is seen. I am content with the sisters, they are good and observant and I hope Saint Anne will always keep us in peace”.

As for the economic situation, the sisters languish. The very benefactors who were most generous no longer are. They would like them to go out collecting alms, but how can they if they are busy in the school?

In this land, though arid, the first vocational flower has blossomed: a young woman asks to become a Daughter of Saint Anne, besides the other two designated by the Bishop.

The Foundress Mother, informed of the precarious situation in which the community found itself, in 1885 comes to the decision to withdraw the sisters who beg alms and the superior. But as often happens, the intervention of the Bishop, who so loved the Institute, and that of influential persons, accompanied by promises, makes her back away from the decision. They continue for some more years.

In 1889, the Municipality, wishing to hire the teacher for the fourth and fifth grades by competition, received a refusal from Mother Rosa, who had no other members available.

Afterwards the girls of the Parish were gathered for catechism, the girls were prepared for First Communion, a schola cantorum and the festive oratory were begun.

The sisters continued only in the nursery school and the workshop for several more years, with considerable sacrifices, especially during the war period.

From 1909 to 1946 three Daughters of Saint Anne sisters also ran the civil hospital, where, besides caring for the eight daily patients, they spent themselves in home care and in looking after the shrine of the “Madonna dei Lumi” attached to the hospital itself.

In the difficult post-war period, unfortunately, no improvements could be made to the premises in need of repair and, therefore, after many vain appeals from the Institute, in Pieve S. Stefano both works ceased: the kindergarten in 1945; the hospital the following year.

23. CASTELVETRANO (TP). Civil Hospital Vittorio Emanuele II - 1883.

The foundation of the Hospital is due to the nobleman Baldassarre Tagliavia and took place in the year 1525, beside the monastery of the Most Holy Annunziata, then the confraternity of S. Gandolfo, from which it took its name. Not many years later it was moved to the premises adjacent to the church of S. Antonio Abate, to whom it was dedicated and where it was housed until 1869, the year in which it was moved to the former convent of the Reformed Fathers of S. Francis, adjacent to the church of the Itria, where it is at present.

At first the Hospital was administered by the noble Company of the Whites; following the regulation of 20 May 1820 it passed to the Municipal Charity Commission and from this to the Congregation of Charity by the law on Pious Works of 3 August 1862 no. 753.

The Municipal Council of Castelvetrano, wishing, in the name of the city, to honor the memory of King Vittorio Emanuele II, in the session of 9 March 1878 resolved that the Institute be named after the ‘Gentleman King’. Since then the Hospital has borne the name of Vittorio Emanuele II.

****************

The Daughters of Saint Anne arrive in Castelvetrano in 1883.

A first verbal approach, concerning the negotiations for their settlement in the Hospital, occurs in 1880, through the priest Don Gioacchino Lentini, who knew of the work of the ‘charitable institution’ of the “Nurses of Palermo”.

The excellent priest had had occasion to visit the Mother house in Piacenza and to address the Foundress directly to have the sisters in his native town.

Commissioned, afterwards, by the Mayor of Castelvetrano, to whom he had many times not failed to speak of the dear and ‘holy institution’, Don Lentini writes to Mother Rosa to ask for the religious for the hospital, where some twenty patients are received, who on certain days dwindle even to five.

Don Gioacchino, on the advice of the good Superior Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi, resident in Palermo, also presents the need to entrust to the sisters the direction of an Institute in which approximately thirty indigent orphan girls are received, from seven years upward (cf. Letter of 12 August 1882).

Mother Gattorno does not delay in replying and in the letter, which bears the date of 08 September 1882, she states the conditions for the maintenance of the Community.

In order to see the beautiful site of the hospital, and so let her touch with her hand the good the sisters could do in Castelvetrano and make their spirit known, Don Lentini had several times invited the Superior Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi to come for a few days to the little town and so have her mediation in obtaining the Daughters of Saint Anne.

I love them, I love the Daughters of Saint Anne very much – he writes to the Foundress Mother –, all the more because I experienced the spirit of sacrifice, self-denial and Christian charity with which they are animated. Precisely when Sr. A. Salvatore and Irene were in my house, a brother of mine, nineteen years old, fell ill with a terrible infectious fever […].

A dense correspondence between the priest and Mother Gattorno reveals the insistence to obtain the religious. He does everything to accept the conditions set by the Institute, already in force in other hospitals. “Everyone is sure – he writes – that the Hospital in the hands of the Daughters of Saint Anne will improve greatly in every respect. I do not doubt it, indeed I am certain that the diligence and Christian charity of the sisters, whom I have known for a long time and admired, will surpass everyone’s expectation”.

The sisters are expected for 1 May 1883. Mother Rosa confirms their arrival for the end of the month.

Four are the sisters assigned to care for the sick women, the patients in the Maternity ward and the children in the foundling home:

Sr. A. Cesira Tonelli (superior) - Sr. A. Erminia - Sr. A. Gaetana - Sr. A. Idelfonsa

Sr. A. Cesira lets several days pass, then, on 25 June 1883, reports to the Mother on the new activity.

The sisters are well and all content. The Administrators themselves admire the unity and concord that can be felt in the small community, where mutual help is evident. Only the superior, who has received the appointment of ‘receiver of foundlings’, is entrusted with the supervision and oversight of the wet nurses, so that the children are well kept. She has seen to drawing up the inventory of the hospital and of the nursing, and asks permission to buy a cotton umbrella to shelter from the scorching rays of the sun.

The sisters are often requested for home care and Sr. A. Cesira, advised by wise and authoritative persons, spares no effort. As for prayers, the timetable cannot be kept; nevertheless, the sisters do not fail, throughout the day, to observe even the smallest religious duties. They are very poor and lacking habits, aprons and shoes, having only one pair, and for this the superior must provide “on behalf of the wretched ones”.

Don Gioacchino Lentini shows himself very caring, providing her with pasta, oil, wood, coal, and sees to it that they lack nothing.

The Hospital is extremely poor, the leftovers are kept for the next day and redistributed. The work is great and the linen for the patients has to be made.

The hospital, over time, had its regular development, especially from the hygienic and sanitary point of view. Its enlargement made it possible to receive a greater number of patients and required the addition of another sister for the pharmacy.

Besides the said aims of assistance to suffering humanity, the Community carried out its work of spiritual good through the teaching of catechism, the spread of the apostleship of prayer, the care and cult of Mary Most Holy of the Itria, with solemn celebrations during Holy Week and on the principal feasts of the liturgical Year.

In June 1956, the Prefectural Commissioner asked for the updating of the Contract and the assignment of two members for hospital service. Given the Hospital’s grave deficit, the monthly payment assigned to each sister would be reduced.

To such proposals not only was the answer negative, but the Generalate put forward the withdrawal of the Community from the hospital, advising the Administration to arrange the replacement with religious of another Congregation. The decisions taken on one side and the resistance on the other slowed the process for some years.

The Daughters of Saint Anne, after overcoming the many difficulties raised by the Administrators, as well as the interventions of authoritative and influential persons, definitively left hospital work on 1 December 1971.

Among the sisters and superiors who succeeded one another in the Hospital of Castelvetrano the superior Sr. A. Serafina Caravita distinguished herself in a particular way, a humble, virtuous, devout, exemplary, charitable sister, scrupulous in the fulfillment of her duties. She died on 27 May 1921, amid the general mourning of all who knew her.

24. ALTAMURA (BA). Civil Hospital - 1883.

The negotiations for the settlement of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Altamura began in 1879 through the interest of the theologian Giambattista de Nora, who, together with three other clerics, looked after the pious place “Monte of the Poor Sick”.

In the letter of 22 June, the priest assured the Mother that the work already under way had sufficient income to supply food, medicines and aid to the sick, as well as the treatment due to the sisters. The correspondence lasted a long time, but with little result.

The interest of that theologian was followed, with a letter dated 24 June 1883, by that of Cav. Candido Turco, who, as President of the Congregation of Charity, renewed the request to Mother Gattorno to obtain four sisters.

The Congregation had obtained possession of the former Convent of the Reformed, called “Madonna delle Grazie”, to use it as a civil Hospital. Located not far from the town, among gardens, it enjoyed healthy air, more temperate than that of the city, where the acute and chronic patients had greatly benefited.

The convent, left abandoned since 1868 and restored to good condition, could receive patients of both sexes.

The Congregation was convinced that “only by entrusting the service to the sisters – able to reconcile exactness and economy – could it reach the desired end and gain credit and that luster proper to a true and proven work of charity!”.

On 26 June the Mother replied that she would send the sisters requested, enclosing a copy of the Rutigliano contract, so that it would be the same. The Congregation of charity did not accept those conditions and an agreement was reached: to pay each sister £. 450, oil and wood.

After further clarifications were requested, on 09 July 1883 the Agreement was stipulated, signed by Cav. Candido Turco and Mother Gattorno.

A few days later it was communicated that the sisters, leaving on 27 August, Monday, at five in the morning, would arrive at Grumo Appula on Tuesday, the 28th, at five in the afternoon.

Sr. A. Emiliana Bellini, the following day, 29 August, writes to the Foundress: “Last evening at nine o’clock we arrived in Altamura. The journey was very fine. At Santo Spirito I met Sr. A. Pacifica and in Bari, getting off the train, the Director, who gave us a warm welcome. We resumed the journey, and when we were near Altamura, another carriage with the Count’s daughters was waiting for us” […].

But here is the surprise. The premises are not ready. The sisters are lodged provisionally in the President’s palace, because it will take some days before the former monks’ cells are put in order. The superior assures the mother that she finds herself among good people, and that she saw to having Mass every day and a confessor. There is a very beautiful church, but the hospital is poor, very different from that of Cortemaggiore. Food is scarce. “There is no wine, no broth… they make a little for lunch and in the evening nothing – she relates – there is no hope that anything will be left over from the hospital… everything will have to be bought”.

A few months later Sr. A. Emiliana fell seriously ill. Mother Gattorno arranged to send another sister to help until she recovered. She did not lack the care and attention of the doctors, among them the director Gaetano Calia, who wrote thus to the Foundress, giving her news of the Superior. “Since September, when she came, she had a cough which she always neglected, until fever set in; in November she was forced to stay in bed… She was a little better and got up… But since, through excessive zeal for the sick and for their service, there is no lack of occasions for catching cold, she fell ill a second time… The left lung works little… there is hope of recovering but not of being perfectly cured… I took the liberty of writing to you because I believe she has never told you her true condition, being unaware of it… (Letter of 30 June 1884).

And some weeks later he added: “Although Sister A. Emiliana has still been in bed, nevertheless her absence is not noticed in the running of the service in the hospital and in the church, so much so that the other sisters are even keeping the month of Saint Anne…” (Letter of 7 July 1884).

Sr. A. Emiliana, despite her worrying state of health, did not give up; she was convinced of her illness and wrote thus to the Mother, on 1 April 1884: “I would like to work for Saint Anne, but if then Jesus should wish to cut short my days, may His will be done”.

The Administration appreciated her qualities and did not intend her to be transferred.

The witness of the sisters soon bore fruit with the first vocations. In fact, in 1884 six fine young women, educated and provided with trousseau and dowry, left for the Postulancy in Rome: the sisters Maria and Chiara Cicirelli, Caterina Patella, Irene Marzulli and the sisters Anna Maria and Veneranda Baldassarre.

The sisters spent themselves in hygienic and medical care for pilgrims and the poor, with a bath service, outpatient services and hospital admission. Any emergency of the city found the sisters in the front line of relief, as happened during the war of 1915-18 and during the Spanish flu epidemic of 1918-19, multiplying themselves with admirable charity and diligence, especially in the numerous cases of meningitis and scarlet fever that occurred.

In 1924 a pharmacy was opened for the free distribution of medicines and in 1932 the ophthalmology ward began to function, followed by that of surgery.

The enlargement of the hospital therefore required an increase in staff and, although the sisters had reached the number of seven, this was not enough to cover all the hospital’s needs.

The Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne, short of members and unable to answer the requests, decided to leave the Administration free to provide otherwise and to withdraw the Community on 14 June 1969.

In granting the “nihil obstat”, the Bishop Mons. Antonio D’Erchia expressed his personal gratitude “for the incalculable good – known only to the Lord and rewardable by Him, accomplished with divine help and with the maternal assistance of the Most Holy Virgin – in over 85 years of residence and generous apostolate in Altamura by the zealous Daughters of Saint Anne”.

25. MONTEPAGANO (TE). Kindergarten - 1883.

The first negotiations between the Mayor of Montepagano, president of the Congregation of Charity, Orazio Mezzopreti, and Mother Rosa Gattorno, for the settlement of the Daughters of Saint Anne in that little town of Abruzzo, bear the date of 4 April 1883.

Three sisters are requested to take care of the Kindergarten and at the same time of a small adjoining hospital with few patients (2 or 3).

Mother Rosa replies that the sisters must be four, two of whom, from time to time, may visit the hospital without, however, taking over its direction.

The conditions are agreed: annual salary of £. 450 for each sister, supply of fuel, furnished house, payment of the journey of arrival.

The sisters, met at Nereto by a member of the Congregation, arrive in Montepagano on 29 August 1883. They are: Sr. A. Della Salette Schiavello, superior; Sr. A. Calasanzia Munari, Sr. Delle Vergini Fugazza and Sr. A. Giulietta Bassi.

On the same day the Superior writes to the Mother, describing in rich detail the hour of arrival, the route marked by a winding ascent, the festive welcome of the population, the sound of the band amid the applause of the people gathered along the sides of the road.

The house is duly furnished: beds with curtains, linen for the sisters and for the kindergarten, objects for use; there are even embroidered curtains at the windows. The house is beautiful – the Superior continues –. On the ground floor there are four rooms, plus kitchen, pantry, toilets and a corridor with sinks. By a beautiful staircase one goes up, where there are four fine rooms for the sisters, with large windows from which to admire the beautiful plains and the stretch of the sea…

Behind the town there is a fine building surrounded by a wall which will serve for the children. Adjoining it there is a small hospital which they will have to take care of later.

Sr. A. Della Salette does not fail to praise the President, whom she considers a noble and wealthy person, “a father”, from whom they will receive many benefits.

A letter of thanks, dated 30 August, written by him, reports great satisfaction at the arrival of the sisters, who at once made a most beautiful impression and won the esteem and affection of the population.

The Kindergarten began its activity on 1 September, but officially the inauguration took place on 13 October with the participation of leading personalities.

The Superior took on the teaching of the first private elementary classes, Sr. A. Calasanzia is in charge of cleaning, Sr. A. Giulietta of the kitchen, Sr. A. Delle Vergini of the Kindergarten.

“I try to keep them content – writes the Superior – but I would like you, Mother, to make them some recommendation, so that they may be more diligent, attentive and take in peace the remarks I shall make. I shall do what I can, but I must remember that I too have a school and cannot spend my time on anything else… Receive these simple sentiments with your usual kindness, asking for your maternal blessing”.

After a few years, the Superior Sr. A. Gerolama Amiel takes over, but she too, in 1886, is recalled by the Mother. The Administration’s displeasure is immediate: it does not agree that the said sister be transferred. “In the short time she has lived in Montepagano – we read in the letter – she has given praiseworthy proofs of industry and intelligence in directing the Kindergarten and to her tireless zeal is due the improvement of the school”. It is asked that the decision be revoked and that the sister return to carry on her arduous and difficult ministry. The letter, dated 12 February 1886, is accompanied by a petition of the citizens to show still more how esteemed the sister was.

Mother Rosa consents to the request: Sr. A. Gerolama returns to Montepagano and remains there until her death, which occurred on 6 June 1899.

The school, thanks to her, had notable development; the children attending the Kindergarten reached the number of 90; the mixed private school was also expanded and a workshop for the girls was also established. On feast days the sisters offered their collaboration to the parish.

Changes of teachers were frequent, but always corresponding to the needs of the place.

Periodically the contract was renewed, since it did not always meet the Community’s needs, above all from the economic point of view. In fact, in 1922, the Mother general gave a first advance notice of wishing to withdraw the sisters from Montepagano. The plea to back down from that decision came immediately from the Congregation of Charity, which promised to improve the situation.

By 1940 the school was no longer as flourishing as before; the sisters lived in rather uncomfortable conditions. After the war period, especially, a financial situation arose for everyone so regrettable that it did not allow the sisters to benefit from the necessary improvements nor even to receive the modest salary that had been paid to them in the years before the war.

From year to year, amid promises, defaults and some concessions in favor of the community, they went on and, from 1951, in a fluctuating way and with few members.

In 1991, by decision of the Mayor of Roseto – on whom it depends – the municipal school is withdrawn from the sisters’ premises. Relations with the authorities are now different, but through the interest of the parish priest, they still enjoy some privileges (electricity and heating oil).

Though precariously and with elderly members, the sisters remain there for over twenty years in service to the Parish, working in parish catechesis and in the surrounding areas, liturgical animation, singing and welcoming children before school hours, thus helping families.

Their work, though actively reduced, is esteemed by the neediest classes and appreciated by the Bishops, who regard it as “a blessing”, the sisters’ premises being a point of reference for youth groups and for the people who turn to them.

However, in 2002, after 119 years of industrious presence, with the gratitude of the entire citizenry, the definitive withdrawal of the religious community from Montepagano takes place.

26. GRAVINA. Hospital “S. Maria del Piede” - 1883.

The negotiations for the coming of the Daughters of Saint Anne to Gravina began in 1880, but were concluded after three years, Giuseppe Gramegna being President of the Congregation of Charity.

The sisters arrived on 18 September 1883, received by the Community of Altamura.

At first, no places being available, they were hosted by the sisters of Ivrea, who ran a nursery school in the town and by whom they were treated with great solicitude and kindness.

After a few days, accompanied by the President, two sisters reached the hospital of Gravina, while the other two remained waiting in Altamura. On 10 October all four settled in the hospital.

Although the patients were few – the hospital had about ten beds – there was much to do to put things in order, prepare and divide the food and distribute medicines to the poor.

The Superior, Sr. A. Filiberta Bertuzzi, through a dense correspondence, from time to time informed the Foundress Mother about the running of the house. All who went to visit the hospital were pleased, finding cleanliness in everything, and she took great satisfaction in the good done by the sisters. She had nothing to complain of and, if things continued thus, the community would give the Mother many consolations.

The sisters needed linen – especially Sr. A. Zaveria, who had left hers at the laundry – and the instruments for “pulling teeth”; about this she asked how to proceed, and on whom lay the obligation of providing them.

Animated by zeal for the salvation of souls, the nurses seized every occasion to exercise their apostolate: preparing the sick to receive the holy sacraments and speaking of the things of holy religion, “glad that the Lord made use of these poor creatures to do great things”.

The Administration was in financial difficulties; salaries were not paid, so that times of sacrifice followed which the religious faced with admirable virtue, so much so that the Mother was asked to establish another community for the Kindergarten.

This second work was begun, but it did not continue. Inconveniences having arisen which, unfortunately, caused the Mother much bitterness, in October 1898 the sisters were withdrawn.

27. VICO PISANO (PS). Municipal school – private school - 1883.

The idea of having a certified sister as teacher in the municipal school of Vicopisano comes from some “fathers of families” fearful that the girls’ class might be entrusted to a not very religious young lady. The task is given to Mr. Mariano Balducci, who personally contacts Mother Rosa Gattorno with a letter of recommendation from the priest Augusto D’Antilio.

The parish priest acts as intermediary between the two parties – the Municipality and the Mother General – so that she may arrange to send three sisters, one for the municipal school and another to start a private school for the girls of the more distinguished families.

The negotiations, which begin in March 1883, continue for several months. The salary fixed by the Municipality amounts to £. 600 a year (little, in the Foundress’s judgment), besides housing. The parish priest, trusting in Providence, assures that the sisters will not have to suffer: with the Municipality’s stipend, the proceeds of private lessons, gifts and alms, at certain times of the year, the deserved remuneration will certainly not be lacking to such worthy workers. The charity of the town will not fail in the task of providing abundantly for all the needs of the sisters (Letter of 02.06.1883).

Don Augusto points out the beauty of the place: “one could not imagine another town better situated. Vicopisano is surrounded by hamlets not far from it. Through the neighboring towns the news of the nuns’ coming has spread and already a general ferment has arisen and a common desire, especially of the distinguished families, to send their little girls to school”.

From a letter of 24 July we learn that an agreement has finally been reached. They ask what to prepare regarding furniture, necessary furnishings, linen, kitchen tools and crockery. The opening of the school is scheduled for 1 October and so it is desired that the sisters arrive by the end of September at the latest. On the 29th, in fact, they reach Vicopisano from Pisa, festively welcomed by the people who were waiting for them. Everything is in order and well prepared for the newcomers.

They are: Sr. A. Del Divino Amore Coppola (Superior), Sr. A. Rosola Guerreri and Sr. A. Vincitrice (teachers) and Sr. A. Tommasa, cook.

The school, inaugurated at the end of October, is attended by about a hundred pupils; on Thursdays and Sundays private lessons are given. Sr. A. Rosola, who is responsible for it, appeals to the Mother to send her more capable help in order to relieve her a little of the burden she bears with difficulty.

Sr. A. Tommasa meets some difficulties and this arouses a touch of concern in the Superior.

A skilled needlework teacher is needed, one who understands everything from knitting to sewing and gold embroidery. This could increase the number of pupils and put the house in more prosperous and flattering conditions.

The parish priest, concluding his letter, invites the Mother – passing through Tuscany – to go to Vicopisano, to visit the house and decide the place to build the chapel. He also thanks her for the gift of the religious, who do very well as regards literary instruction, but not so as regards women’s crafts (Letter of 1.12.1883).

The start of the Community struggles to take off and even collapses with the transfer of Sr. A. Rosola.

Not having been able to arrange the sending of a needlework teacher and the return of Sr. A. Rosola forces the Mother General to withdraw the four sisters at the end of July 1884.
