28. MONTEMURLO (FI). Municipal Elementary Schools - 1883.

The Mayor of Montemurlo (FI), in June 1883, had announced a competition to hire the teaching staff for the town’s municipal Schools.

The chaplain of the Pieve, Don Venceslao Tonini, having got wind of it, hastened to express to him his wish and that of the whole population to entrust, that is, the instruction of the girls to the sisters Daughters of Saint Anne.

To achieve his aim better, on 2 July he went to the superior of the House of Florence, Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, who advised him to put the project to Mother Gattorno.

On the same day he wrote to Mother Rosa, describing the place to her in the minutest detail. “A pleasant spot at the foot of the mountain, with very healthy air. The house intended for the sisters stands about half a kilometer from the Pieve; nearby there is a chapel where Mass is celebrated once a week, but on feast days it will be indispensable to reach the parish. Religious assistance to the sisters is assured in every respect through the availability of three priests, always present”.

The request is very precise. Two teachers with a higher-grade diploma are needed: one for the girls over eight years old; the other should go to the hamlet, about half a kilometer from the house, for the convenience of the population, to teach the little ones, boys and girls.

The dwelling comprises five rooms; it is surrounded by a meadow that could be turned into a vegetable garden, enclosed by a high wall and a gate; the classroom is quite spacious and well ventilated. This will be temporary, since the Municipality has resolved to build a new house for this purpose.

To this pleasant description he adds the other conditions: the annual salary assigned by the Municipality amounts to £. 1000, but after some years, seeing the pupils’ progress, it could be raised to a higher figure.

It is not excluded that the sisters might also be paid by the pupils, as they have done in the past… In short, “they would gladly stay and manage very well” – we read in the letter – also counting on the protection of several illustrious Ladies, among them the Marchioness Mrs. Carolina Covoni of Florence.

Mother Rosa’s reply is positive, but on condition that to the allowance be added: oil, wood, wheat and wine for the whole year.

The negotiations continue with the plea of the parish priest, who finds the conditions onerous and cannot accept them; he assures, however, that afterwards, when the Municipality has seen the girls’ progress, it will be courteous with some increase.

The correspondence is interwoven very frequently. In it emerge Tonini’s insistence, to whom the realization of his project matters very much, and the Mother’s resistance, to the point of leading the good priest to write to her in these terms: “This is a town where the sisters are desired and everyone will be most grateful […]. See if you can satisfy a poor priest who is deeply committed to this matter… I ask it in the name of Saint Anne. Satisfy me and all this population, let us do it for love of Jesus and He will open all the roads for us. Satisfy me, rev. Mother, and you will see that you too will be fully satisfied” (Letter of 21.07.1883). An agreement is finally reached. The opening of the school is scheduled for 2 November 1883.

The sisters assigned to Montemurlo are already ready and are in Florence: Sr. A. della Risurrezione Militello, Superior, Sr. Fortunata Zaccherini and Sr. A. Bianchina Andreoli (teachers) and the fourth, Sr. A. Gervasia Marini, will be in charge of the kitchen.

Having obtained the regular appointment from the Municipal Council, the sisters arrive in Montemurlo toward the end of October 1883, accompanied by Sr. A. Santina Solenghi and with the pastoral blessing of the Bishop of Pistoia, who recommends to Don Venceslao to take care of the religious, who “are a blessing for the whole town”.

On 17 December 1883, the Curate writes to the Mother about the welcome received by the four religious from the Mayor and the municipal Secretary. They are loved – he says – by all the people and in particular by the excellent Mrs. Irene Cherardi, who has taken them under her great protection and helps them in many things.

The opening of the school, postponed to 10 December, is attended by a good number of girls, who together with their parents are very happy.

Sr. A. Bianchina has to go every morning to the school, far from the house, and this arouses concern in Mother Rosa, who asks the superior how long the sister takes to cover the road and recommends that she not go alone. She is accompanied by another (the cook) and this means two being absent, with a consequent overload for the superior, who must also take on the kitchen work. To remedy the inconvenience, the parish priest, who has also become the community’s confessor, arranges for Sr. A. Bianchina to go with a 12-year-old pupil, well known to him. The road is safe – the superior confirms – little traveled and requires about 18 minutes to reach the school (Letter of 15.12.1883).

Sr. A. della Risurrezione, in the following letter of 30.12.1883, informs the Mother of other details.

“Having arrived at Montemurlo, the priest Don Venceslao, ‘all bustling with contentment’, led us to the Town Hall to present us to the Mayor and the Secretary, designating the superior and the teachers, giving us, separately, advice on how to conduct ourselves…

We are settled as best we can be – she writes –. There is a room with four little beds, a small trunk with a little linen, new and partly used, and other objects for our use, a room decked out for the school, a smaller one for needlework and another little room that will serve as the kitchen… Despite this we are content all the same, beyond what they have done would be too much. They give us much courage, telling us to be patient for now, that afterwards, little by little, we shall have everything. I can only tell you, O my dear Mother, that there is an air of paradise that gives us such an appetite that one would digest iron. We have begun to visit our benefactresses, by whom we were well received. They are the ‘leading ladies’ of the town. Every day each one brings her little gift: one flour, another tomatoes, fruit, etc. We hope that with Saint Anne’s help the schools will go well, that the sisters may gain from it for the honor of the Institute first and then to leave the whole town content… so they may be fonder of us” […]. To leave the population happier, I teach the older girls although it is a great sacrifice, and I hope we shall be rewarded, because they are very grateful… though the reward for toil is not to be expected from the people of the world, but from God”.

Sr. A. della Risurrezione goes on at length in the letter, saying that the sisters are without aprons and shoes, and that she herself has shoes so broken she cannot walk and for the moment cannot provide for such needs, because they have not received the monthly salary. She feels distressed because the church is far away and they can attend Mass and receive communion once a week, only on Sunday “like lay people”. She says she is ready, however, to offer such sacrifice to the Lord, because obedience works miracles. She asks for prayers to make up for what they lack and the blessing for herself and the sisters.

When everything had been set going with satisfaction and contentment on the part of the families and the Municipal Council, here is the first transfer: the Superior is called to Piacenza by Mother Rosa and never returned to Montemurlo. The following year, without any advance notice to the school Authority, Sr. A. Bianchina Andreoli left: she had fallen ill from her going back and forth to the distant school.

The parish priest, who had warmly urged the settlement of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Montemurlo, is seriously reprimanded by the Mayor for the sister’s departure at a thoroughly unfavorable moment and one that cannot be accepted. He therefore turns to the Mother to send back the teacher and, if she wishes to transfer her, to wait for the end of the school year. Mother Rosa confirms the transfer of Sr. A. Bianchina and announces the arrival of another sister.

In a short time three titular teachers were changed. The reason was always poor health, so that the transfers happened suddenly and to the surprise of the municipal Representatives and of the competent Body.

Such conduct, certainly not respectful of the laws, ended up annoying the Mayor, who did not fail to express his discontent. The Institute, yes, had made great sacrifices to maintain the religious’ presence in the town, but no less had been those of the Municipality, which, meanwhile, had tried to ease things for them, keeping their post, besides having raised the Superior’s salary by £. 100 for teaching sewing and knitting.

Between 1887 and 1889 the letters from the municipal Authority take on an indignant and resentful tone; they are somewhat threatening and make note of the irregularities that kept recurring because of the continual transfer of teachers during the current school year.

In a note of 7 May 1889 we read: “Just as the Municipality cannot dismiss a teacher on the spot, so the teacher cannot leave the school on the spot. The Municipality is tired of this continual and frequent change of teachers, of this excessive and unseemly instability”.

When the examinations are over, at the end of July 1889, the sisters leave Montemurlo.

It is the Mayor himself who advises Mother Rosa to give up the two schools entrusted to them, to withdraw the two teaching sisters, citing the distance of the school from the residence, as well as the distance from the church. (Letter 09.06.1889).

29. ALTAMURA (BA). Pious Work “Monte of the Poor”.

The Daughters of Saint Anne had been settled in Altamura for only a few months when the Bishop Mons. Luigi M. Pellegrini, sensitive to the situation of poverty, resuming negotiations, asks Mother Gattorno for four more religious to look after the sick at home. The sisters are not to depend on the lay Administration, but exclusively on the Church, their Mother.

As for furnishing, four beds are needed, with their respective bedposts, winter and summer covers, which the Foundress is to supply; the mattresses and furniture will be provided by the Administration, composed of four ecclesiastics.

The Bishop, who cares deeply about the “Monte of the Poor”, is generous with promises: the sisters will lack nothing, they will be received with every consideration, as befits religious who spend themselves in charity for the poor.

On 4 September 1883, Mother Rosa replies that everything will be provided and asks for the money for the journey.

In the first days of November the sisters arrive in Altamura.

To avoid misunderstandings, Canon Saverio Genco restates the reasons why the sisters were called: care of the sick at home. Their task is to visit and assist the poor sick of the city, supply food and medicines, relieving their misery through charitable work.

At present the sisters are lodged in the Bishop’s Palace; the commission strives to ensure nothing is lacking, hoping that next year they will have a house of their own.

Of the four sisters it is requested that one be trained for the pharmacy, considered indispensable for economy and saving for the benefit of the poor sick.

The superior is Sr. A. Primitiva Boresi, full of good will and eager to work for the glory of God; she is assisted by Sr. A. Ortensia, Sr. A. Crescenziana and Sr. A. Zelinda, all young sisters and inexperienced for the work required.

At first, Sr. A. Primitiva seems dissatisfied, because there are no sick people. She asks for information on whether there are any in the homes, because the sisters – she says – are ready to keep vigil even at night, but no one asks for them. Four are too many and for the work only two would be enough.

After a few months, the news is very different. “Now – she writes on 19.12.1884 – the sick are increasing and so we shall do something for the glory of God and the honor of the Institute. Sr. A. Zelinda knows how to pull teeth, but she does not have the instruments; those of the commission would be glad if this too were done but I do not know who should see to the instruments”.

Sr. A. Primitiva completes her letter wishing happy holidays to the Mother, to Fr. Tornatore and to the secretaries.

Besides home care, the sisters are entrusted by the Bishop with teaching catechism in the parish church, on Thursdays and Sundays.

The sick exceed the number of 50. In a short time the network of relief widens and the need arises to establish a pharmacy for the distribution of medicines to all the poor of the city.

The Mother succeeded in providing the competent sister for this office and everything went on for the best, answering the deep humanitarian aspirations, which the sick perceived and expressed to her their gratitude. Let us hear one of them: Filippo Giffi:

“…It seems to me today that I see all the sick saved by the Daughters of Saint Anne file religiously past in your presence and, with hands on their breast, burst into a cry: Rosa Gattorno, the sick saved by your work salute you and pray for your preservation!

O yes, the work that is bound to your name makes it remain imprinted on the heart of all.

Oh, how many times in the silent hours of the night, at the monotonous ticking of the clock, whose turns seem so slow to the sick, seeing at my bedside the Sister wholly intent on being a relief and comfort to me, my mind has flown to you, so deserving of the sick, and I have wept for joy at the thought that sublime is the self-denial of her who, raised in the comforts and softness of life, spends everything and abandons everything so that suffering brothers may feel less the weight of misfortune…”. (Letter of 28.08.1885).

Joys and sorrows alternated, making the Foundress’s life rich and prodigious. In that same year 1885 she received a letter of accusations against the service the religious were giving and then, after taking due precautions, she changed the personnel. This displeased the Administration, which made several insistent requests to obtain back the first Superior, Sr. A. Primitiva.

This attitude, which hindered freedom of movement, caused the withdrawal of the Community in 1888.

The Daughters of Saint Anne in Altamura also ran the Home (1893 - 1959) and the “S. Lucia Conservatory” (1898 – 1918).

30. BISTAGNO (AL). Kindergarten – Workshop 1883.

It is the priest Don Ludovico Bisio, Vicar forane and parish priest of Nizza Monferrato who, in February 1883, acts as go-between for the parish priest Fr. Michele Tagliafico and Mother Rosa, to obtain the religious and set up the Kindergarten in the Piedmontese town of Bistagno.

Three sisters are requested: two teachers and one for the duties of servant-cook. The allowance amounts to £. 1,100, including the small expenses of wood and light. For the moment the Administration provides the furnishings for the rooms and the kitchen; afterwards it will provide whatever is needed (but in reality it will be the sisters who complete the furnishing, with their resourcefulness, beginning with the beds with their linen, furniture for the house and kitchen utensils).

The sisters are expected to arrive in Bistagno on 16 November 1883 (Letter of 10.11.1883)

Mother Rosa, who had experienced Don Bisio’s help and zeal, did not delay in replying affirmatively, sending four sisters: Sr. A. Crispina Callini, Superior, Sr. A. Clarice Traversi and Sr. A. Brigida Luciani, teachers, and Sr. A. Orsolina Garibaldi, cook.

On 21 December 1883, the archpriest of Bistagno thanks the Mother for the sisters who have been sent for the Kindergarten. “The superior Sr. A. Crispina – he writes – is distinguished by her zeal, activity and prudence in giving the Kindergarten a good course; Sr. A. Clarice is wholly engaged in teaching the children, Sr. A. Brigida is the idol of the girls attending the private school […]. In less than a month they have brought the teaching to a level that one would not believe unless one saw and touched it. The population of Bistagno too is delighted with these good daughters so active, industrious and wise and at the same time good and prudent […]. They justly enjoy the good esteem and respect of every category of persons in this town”. And he thanks also in the name of the Mayor.

“The house of Bistagno is going full sail – wrote, satisfied, the parish priest Tagliafico, on 29 March 1884 –. The pupils of the Kindergarten exceed a hundred and the private school gives a quite considerable contingent”. He also points out how necessary it would be to set up a boarding school to receive the girls from the surrounding towns and entrust them to the Daughters of Saint Anne. From this one can deduce how much, in a short time, the sisters were esteemed for their bearing, their religious conduct and their sacrifices for the good of the pupils. In the same letter the good priest invites the Mother to go to Bistagno for the inauguration of the little chapel, for which the Superior Crispina is preparing the older pupils for a small entertainment.

The sisters’ commitment (also in the municipal schools), so evident, was rewarded with praise and applause during the end-of-year performance. All who attended were truly satisfied, indeed amazed at the success of the show, carried out with fine grace, skill and confidence by the little ones, the boys and the girls who performed with songs, dialogues and recitation.

Most beautiful is the testimony of Don Giuseppe Mollo, who for the occasion was in Bistagno, his native town.

He writes thus on 3 August 1883: “I did not know, and cannot explain to myself how in a few months these tender children have made such progress. I, who know the town, know that the children were left to themselves and that coarseness was their chief character. Now to find them so disciplined, all hanging on the glance and slightest sign of the sister teacher […] each sustaining his own part in very long and variously interwoven dialogues was for me a real spectacle, in which I could only admire the blessing of the Lord manifest in its effects and the heroic patience of these good Daughters of Saint Anne, who knew well how, in a few months, to produce this unexpected change”.

All seemed to go well until 1922. The numerical decline of pupils and the low attendance that later came about no longer guaranteed the means of subsistence for the sisters, although they worked hard with private lessons in music and embroidery. As a result, in 1927 the Mother general, Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, began the procedure for withdrawing the community. With the Administration’s promise to improve the treatment of the sisters and increase the school population, and also thanks to the keen interest of the archpriest Don G. Lerma, who did not want to be deprived of the sisters’ presence, the decision was revoked. More respectful contractual conditions followed, with payment more in line with the community’s needs, besides making use of the income from private lessons.

That of the Daughters of Saint Anne in Bistagno was an animating presence that conformed ever better to the needs of the ecclesial Community, devoting itself to parish catechesis and to the Associations: Daughters of Mary and Catholic Action.

So they went on until 1960, when the Provincial Superior Sr. A. Celsa Farinelli, citing the scarcity of religious personnel, asked the bishop of Acqui for the nihil obstat for the withdrawal of the community, which took place on 30 December 1960, according to the plan for scaling down the Works foreseen by the Congregation. The decision was received with deep regret by the parish priest Don Giuseppe La Piana.

31. PALERMO. Fernandez Infirmary - 1883.

Palazzo Fernandez stands in Via Papireto in the Seralcadio or Monte di Pietà. It was built in part as an Infirmary at the beginning of the nineteenth century by Giovanni Fernandez on an acquired plot.

Now, duly restored, it houses the Fine Arts.

***************

The Daughters of Saint Anne had been running Houses in Palermo since 1880.

The Revv. Parish Priests: Bernardo Cataliotti del Grano (universal heir), Angelo Bernava and Francesco Mazzola, trusted executors of the estate of Giovanni Fernandez, in fulfillment of the Testator’s last wishes, founded this Infirmary for poor gentlewomen of the city.

The work, in 1883, was entrusted to the Daughters of Saint Anne: a Community of three sisters who for many years exercised their apostolate in the humblest silence and in the practice of every religious virtue.

The Great War of 1915-18 and the immediate post-war period drew our Sisters out of the shadows to expose them, through exceptional activity, laden with sacrifices of every kind, to the praise of the Authorities and the gratitude of the citizenry.

They, in fact, were requested and employed in the economy kitchens, permanent and temporary, in the city and the surroundings, so that from 1915 to September 1918, at the commission of the Most Illustrious Princess of Fitalia, president of the Catholic Ladies, they prepared soup for the children of the conscripts housed in an Asylum in the city.

When the Spanish flu broke out, in September 1918 and throughout the epidemic, by order of the Mayor of the city, they supplied 13,600 rations of light soup in broth and 13,600 rations of meat and in November of the same year 30,878 soups to the poor.

Simultaneously, from 1917, the Most Illustrious Prince of Valdarno, Ettore Mineo, Director of the Economy Kitchens, entrusted to them a permanent Economy Kitchen in the city for supplying 1000 soups a day and another temporary one, lasting ten months, in the Malaspina Quarter, and from November 1918 to May 1919 yet another at Sferracavallo, in the surroundings of Palermo. Another assignment they received from the American Red Cross, for which they also prepared the daily soup for about 500 children of conscripts housed at Villa Filippina.

All this work demanded an uninterrupted, day-long sacrifice, both for the toil itself and for the discomforts arising from life outside the house and from having to go from one place to another, several times a day, braving the rigors of the seasons.

In 1931, the flood that struck the city on 21-22 February damaged the building, so that it was necessary to move the Infirmary temporarily to other rented premises.

The work then returned to its premises, restored on that occasion, and took on new vigor there.

A few years later, precisely in 1933, the Committee of the Protection of Young Women, having of necessity to vacate the premises of the little convent of S. Marco, in which young women in need of help were housed, asked the Administration of the Fernandez Infirmary to be willing to receive them temporarily. The hospitality, however, became permanent, so that from then on the sisters’ field of apostolate extended, onto rather arid and stony ground, but one also fruitful of good.

The Daughters of Saint Anne continued its service until 1943.

32. CACCIVIO (CO). Kindergarten – Workshop.

Don Giacomo Pedoja, fervent parish priest of Caccivio, was the promoter of the work established there, following the holographic will in which Cav. Giuseppe Rubini, who died in Dongo (CO) on 18 September 1880, had provided a bequest of £. 1000 in favor of a Kindergarten to be built within ten years of his death.

The Rubini brothers, in memory of their father, the following year gave impetus to the initiative with the approval of the Municipal Council.

The idea, thus well encouraged and answering a felt need of the population of Caccivio, was put into practice thanks to a zealous Provisional Commission, of which the parish priest Pedoja was also a member.

In 1883, following the contractual agreements, again through the interest of the said priest, Mother Rosa granted four sisters for the direction of the Kindergarten.

The religious assigned there – Sr. A. Bianca Branchi, Sr. A. Apollonia, Sr. A. Ermete Cardosi and Sr. A. Pietosa – soon saw hundreds of children flock in, enjoying wide sympathy from the whole population of Caccivio, becoming, at all times, the object of private charity from the most respectable and well-off families of the town. Even today the generosity of the donors is tied to the memory of deceased persons.

To this first branch of apostolate others followed: catechetical instruction, the municipal elementary school, the workshop and, temporarily, during the war of 1915-18, free instruction of the children of conscripts and of little refugees, to whom the school meal was always distributed.

Mother Gattorno visited this Kindergarten in its early days and, rejoicing at the rapid development of the work, wished the Most Blessed sacrament to be kept in the sisters’ private chapel. Congratulating then the young girls received there, she prophesied to many of them that they would be her religious daughters. In fact, more than 50 followed the vocation as she had foretold, among them some

great missionaries.

Among the sisters who worked for a long time in Caccivio, Sr. A. Mattia Viterbo, an elementary school teacher for over 40 years, is still remembered today.

At present the sisters who make up the community, besides running the Nursery School, take an active part in parish life and look after the festive Oratory.

The Nursery School of Caccivio, with several sections run by lay teachers, is clearly a service to the whole citizenry, with aims and programs directed at the integral education of children, with a flexible and open educational path, modifiable according to changes in the operating situation and the child’s interests, respecting the school calendar.

The building, enlarged over time, today presents itself with wide interior and exterior spaces, in compliance with regulations and answering the needs of welcome and serenity, of movement, of safety, of stimulating the pupils’ curiosity and learning.

The Administrative Council, which looks after the economic aspects, attentive to less well-off families, establishes from time to time the criteria for enrollments and fees, which are supplemented by a municipal subsidy.

The Nursery School has a Statute, which sets the rules for its running and the related initiatives.
